q: Debra buys a used sofa for $150 at her neighbor Lou's garage sale. Neither Debra nor Lou has ever sold furniture before. A week later the sofa's frame collapses, and Debra sues, claiming the sofa didn't conform to Lou's statement that it was “solid oak, never repaired.” Lou moves to dismiss, arguing that Article 2 doesn't govern a sale between two consumers. How should the court rule?
o: Deny the motion: Article 2 governs transactions in goods whether or not either party is a merchant.
Grant the motion: Article 2 applies only when at least one party is a merchant.
Grant the motion: a sale under $500 falls outside Article 2 and is governed by the common law.
Deny the motion, but only because Lou made an express statement; without one, the common law would govern.
oe: Correct. Article 2's scope turns on the subject matter (goods) and the transaction (a sale), not on who the parties are. Consumer-to-consumer sales are covered (Problem 1-4: the garage-sale sofa). Merchant status matters only for particular rules such as firm offers, § 2-207(2), and § 2-314.
No provision limits Article 2's scope to merchant transactions. That's a classic trap: merchant status decides whether certain rules apply, not whether the Article applies.
The $500 figure is the statute of frauds threshold in § 2-201(1). It decides whether a signed record is needed, not whether Article 2 governs.
Article 2 governs the sale either way. Lou's statement matters to whether there's an express warranty (§ 2-313), not to scope.
topic: Wk 1 · The UCC & which law governs — Scope and merchant status

q: Bridget buys a 1908 $10 “Indian Eagle” gold coin from a coin dealer for $1,500, paying with a debit card. When an appraiser later says the coin has been polished and is worth far less, Bridget sues the dealer under Article 2. The dealer argues that money is excluded from the definition of “goods.” Is the coin a good?
o: Yes: only money used to pay the price is excluded, and the coin is what's being sold.
No: anything that is or was legal tender is excluded from “goods” under § 2-105(1).
No: the coin is a thing in action because its value depends on the collector market.
Yes, but only because Bridget paid with a debit card rather than with other coins.
oe: Correct. Section 2-105(1) excludes “the money in which the price is to be paid.” A collectible coin bought as a commodity is the subject matter of the sale, so it is a good (Problem 1-1(B)).
The exclusion is narrower. It reaches only the money used to pay the price, not currency or coins that are themselves the subject of the sale.
A thing in action is an intangible right, such as a right to sue or collect. A physical coin is a movable thing.
How the buyer paid doesn't matter. The coin is a good because it is the thing sold, not the price.
topic: Wk 1 · The UCC & which law governs — Collectible money

q: Adroit Industries enters into four contracts in the same week. Which contract is most clearly a transaction in goods under § 2-105(1)?
o: A contract to buy 400 tanks of medical oxygen for its hospital clients.
A contract to buy 1,000 certificated shares of Microsoft stock from a broker.
A contract to buy 50 state lottery tickets for an office raffle.
A contract to have 100,000 yen credited to its brokerage account.
oe: Correct. Gases and liquids are movable things, so oxygen in tanks is a good (Problem 1-1(A)).
Investment securities are expressly excluded from goods and are governed by Article 8, even when certificated and held in hand.
A lottery ticket is a thing in action, a right to claim a prize, and things in action are excluded.
A credit entry in an account isn't a movable thing. It is a financial asset or thing in action, not tangible currency.
topic: Wk 1 · The UCC & which law governs — What counts as goods

q: Cheyenne Industries owns a tract of land. It signs two contracts with Buyer. In the first, Buyer may enter and cut the standing timber. In the second, Buyer may drill for and extract the oil and gas beneath the tract. Which contract is a contract for the sale of goods under Article 2?
o: Only the timber contract: timber is goods whoever cuts it; oil and gas only if the seller extracts.
Both, because each involves things that will be movable once they are removed from the land.
Only the oil and gas contract, because liquids and gases are movable things.
Neither, because both involve things attached to real property, which Article 2 never covers.
oe: Correct. Under § 2-107(2), timber to be cut and growing crops are goods whether the buyer or the seller severs them. Under § 2-107(1), minerals including oil and gas are goods only if they are to be severed by the seller; a buyer's right to extract is an interest in land.
Being movable after severance isn't enough for minerals. Section 2-107(1) requires severance by the seller.
Oil and gas can be goods, but only when the seller extracts them. Here the buyer will drill.
Section 2-107 brings some things attached to realty within Article 2. Timber is goods regardless of who cuts it.
topic: Wk 1 · The UCC & which law governs — Things attached to realty

q: Variation: Cheyenne instead sells Buyer a small storage building on the tract. Under the contract, Cheyenne's own crew will lift the building off its foundation and put it on skids, and Buyer will haul it away. Is this a sale of goods?
o: Yes: a structure to be removed from realty is goods when the seller severs it.
No: buildings are real property, and moving one doesn't change that.
Yes, but only if the building can be removed without material harm to the land.
No: a structure becomes goods only if the buyer severs it and takes the risk of removal.
oe: Correct. Section 2-107(1) treats a structure or its materials to be removed from realty as goods if they are to be severed by the seller (Problem 1-1(C), the Lumber Yard building).
Section 2-107(1) expressly covers structures to be removed from realty when the seller severs them.
The material-harm test belongs to § 2-107(2) (crops and other severable things). For structures, the question is who severs.
It is the reverse. Structures and minerals are goods when the seller severs them.
topic: Wk 1 · The UCC & which law governs — Structures severed by the seller
pre: Cheyenne Industries owns a tract of land. It signs two contracts with Buyer. In the first, Buyer may enter and cut the standing timber. In the second, Buyer may drill for and extract the oil and gas beneath the tract. Which contract is a contract for the sale of goods under Article 2?

q: Able needs cash. It “sells” a painting to Baker for $100,000 under a bill of sale, and in the same document agrees to repurchase the painting in 12 months for $110,000. Baker never displays the painting, and the parties agree Baker won't benefit if it rises in value or lose if it falls. When Able defaults on the repurchase, which law governs Baker's rights in the painting?
o: Article 9, because the “sale” operates only to create a security interest.
Article 2, because the parties signed a bill of sale and called the deal a sale.
Article 2A, because Able kept an interest in getting the painting back.
The common law of contracts, because a repurchase agreement is not a transaction in goods.
oe: Correct. Section 2-102(3)(a) excludes a transaction that operates only to create a security interest. Baker bears neither depreciation nor appreciation, so economically this is a secured loan governed by Article 9.
Labels don't control scope. Parties can't make Article 2 apply to a disguised security interest by calling it a sale.
Article 2A governs true leases of goods. A repurchase arrangement with a fixed return is a financing device, not a lease.
Paintings are goods, and secured transactions in goods are governed by Article 9, not the common law.
topic: Wk 1 · The UCC & which law governs — Disguised security interest

q: Within one month, Ortiz Construction (1) leases three forklifts for two years, (2) receives a used generator as a gift from a retiring contractor, and (3) inherits a backhoe under its founder's will. A dispute arises over the forklifts' condition. Which body of law governs the forklift dispute?
o: Article 2A, the article on leases of goods.
Article 2, because forklifts are goods.
Article 9, because the lessor keeps an ownership interest in the forklifts.
The common law, because Article 2 covers only sales and the forklifts weren't sold.
oe: Correct. On the governing-law chart, the goods column runs: sale → Article 2 (or the CISG); lease → Article 2A; security interest → Article 9; gift → common law; bequest → law of wills. The four factors are examined in order: subject matter, rights transferred, location of the parties, and the parties' agreement.
Goods alone don't decide it. The second factor, the nature of the rights transferred, points to Article 2A for a lease.
Article 9 governs security interests. A true lease isn't one, and nothing suggests a disguised security interest.
There is a statute for leases of goods: Article 2A. The common law governs the gift of the generator, not the lease.
topic: Wk 1 · The UCC & which law governs — Governing-law chart

q: Botticelli wrote and designed an art book and hired Speedy Offset, a commercial printer, to print and bind 500 copies to Botticelli's specifications. Botticelli claims Speedy printed the pages below industry standards and bound them badly. Speedy argues the deal was for services, so Article 2 doesn't apply. Under the 2022 version of § 2-102, what is the best analysis?
o: Article 2 applies: manufacturing services count as goods, and the claims concern the books' conformity.
Article 2 doesn't apply: the value of the work lies in Speedy's printing skill, so services predominate and the common law governs everything.
Article 2 applies only to the binding claim, because binding is a physical process and printing is a service.
Article 2 applies only if Botticelli proves the paper and ink cost more than half of the total price.
oe: Correct. The comments attribute services used to manufacture goods to the goods side, and the design work was Botticelli's own. Goods likely predominate, so Article 2 applies. Even if they didn't, § 2-102(2)(a) applies the goods-related provisions, such as warranties and rejection, to a claim about the books' quality (Problem 1-2).
Manufacturing services are attributed to the goods. And after 2022, even when services predominate, goods-related provisions such as warranties still apply.
Both printing and binding are part of producing the books, which are specially manufactured goods. The claims don't split this way.
Relative value is one factor in deciding predominance, not a threshold. And goods-related provisions apply even if goods don't predominate.
topic: Wk 1 · The UCC & which law governs — Hybrid: printing and binding

q: A custom-home builder agrees to build an addition for $200,000; about 60% of the price is labor and 40% materials, including kitchen cabinets the builder buys and installs. Assume services predominate. The owner sues on two theories: (1) the cabinets were defective, breaching the implied warranty of merchantability; and (2) the builder broke an oral promise to add a $9,000 skylight, which the builder says is unenforceable for lack of a signed record under § 2-201. Under amended § 2-102(2), which Article 2 provisions apply?
o: The warranty provisions apply to the cabinets, but § 2-201 does not apply to the transaction.
Neither applies, because when services predominate Article 2 doesn't apply to any part of the transaction.
Both apply, because any transaction that includes goods is entirely governed by Article 2.
Section 2-201 applies, but the warranty claim must proceed under the common law of services.
oe: Correct. When the sale-of-goods aspects don't predominate, only provisions relating primarily to the goods apply: warranties, tender, risk of loss, acceptance, rejection, and cure, and buyer's remedies for nonconforming goods. Provisions about the transaction as a whole, such as § 2-201, the formation rules, and § 2-209, don't apply.
That was the old predominant-purpose result. The 2022 amendments apply the goods-related provisions even when services predominate.
Only when goods predominate does Article 2 govern the transaction as a whole. Here they don't.
It is the reverse. Warranties relate primarily to the goods; § 2-201 relates to the transaction as a whole.
topic: Wk 1 · The UCC & which law governs — Hybrid: which provisions apply

q: In a state that hasn't adopted the 2022 amendments, a pool company installs an in-ground pool, including a diving board. Labor makes up most of the price. A swimmer is injured when the diving board's surface proves dangerously slick, and the buyer sues for breach of the implied warranty of merchantability. The court follows Anthony Pools v. Sheehan. What result?
o: Article 2's warranty applies, because the claim concerns the diving board, a good.
Article 2 doesn't apply, because the predominant purpose of the contract was the provision of services.
Article 2 applies to the entire transaction, including claims about poor workmanship in digging the pool.
Article 2 applies only if the contract separately stated the price of the diving board.
oe: Correct. Under the gravamen test, the court asks whether the claim concerns the goods or the services. The defective diving board is a good, so Article 2's implied warranty applies even though services predominated.
That is the predominant-purpose test, which Anthony Pools declined to apply to a claim about the goods themselves.
The gravamen test splits by claim. A claim about defective excavation work would be about services.
A price allocation may matter to predominance, but the gravamen test looks at what the claim is about.
topic: Wk 1 · The UCC & which law governs — Gravamen of the claim

q: In a state applying the traditional predominant-purpose test to a contract to supply and install a commercial walk-in freezer, the court asks whether Article 2 governs. Which consideration is NOT one of the factors courts use?
o: Whether the buyer is a consumer rather than a business.
The language of the contract, such as whether it speaks of “purchase” or of “services.”
The nature of the supplier's business, such as whether it regularly sells freezers.
The relative value of the freezer compared with the installation labor.
oe: Correct. That's not a factor. The factors are the contract language, the nature of the supplier's business, the relative value of the goods and services, and whether it makes sense to apply Article 2. (The 2022 comments add the parties' purposes.)
The contract's language is a recognized factor.
The supplier's business is a recognized factor.
Relative value of goods and services is a recognized factor; under the 2022 comments an agreed allocation is ordinarily binding.
topic: Wk 1 · The UCC & which law governs — Predominant purpose factors

q: A Seattle equipment maker sells to customers in the United States, Canada, and Mexico. It wants Washington's version of Article 2 to govern every sale. Its form says only: “This contract is governed by the law of the State of Washington.” What is the most significant problem with the clause?
o: It doesn't exclude the CISG, which is part of Washington law for cross-border sales.
Parties can't choose governing law in a sale of goods; the court must apply the law of the buyer's location.
The CISG applies only to consumer sales, so the clause is unnecessary for business customers.
The clause must name a specific section of Article 2 to be effective.
oe: Correct. For a sale to a Canadian or Mexican business, choosing “Washington law” may pull in the CISG. The clause should choose Washington law and expressly exclude the CISG (Problem 1-6).
Parties may agree on governing law; the agreement is the fourth of the four factors.
It is the opposite. The CISG excludes consumer sales and applies to commercial sales between parties in different contracting nations.
No such rule exists. The defect is the failure to exclude the CISG.
topic: Wk 1 · The UCC & which law governs — CISG and choice of law

q: A buyer sues a seller of a used tractor, alleging that the seller knowingly lied about the tractor's hours of use to induce the sale and that the buyer was a minor when he signed. The seller argues that Article 2 contains no fraud or capacity provisions, so those defenses aren't available in a sale of goods. Is the seller right?
o: No: unless a Code provision displaces them, fraud and capacity rules supplement the UCC.
Yes: Article 2 is a complete code, so any doctrine it doesn't mention is preempted.
Partly: fraud supplements the Code, but capacity is displaced because the UCC defines “person.”
No, but only because the buyer is a consumer; between merchants the Code would displace these defenses.
oe: Correct. Section 1-103(b) keeps common-law doctrines such as capacity, agency, estoppel, fraud, duress, and mistake in play unless a specific provision displaces them (as § 2-207 displaces the mirror-image rule).
The UCC is not comprehensive and is rarely the only law that applies. Section 1-103(b) says so expressly.
Capacity to contract is one of the doctrines § 1-103(b) names as supplementing the Code.
Section 1-103(b) applies to all parties. Merchant status doesn't change it.
topic: Wk 1 · The UCC & which law governs — Common law supplements the Code

q: Counsel in a sales dispute relies on an Official Comment to Article 2 that seems to conflict with the text of the section as enacted by the state legislature, which adopted a non-uniform version. Counsel also cites a decision from another state's highest court interpreting the uniform text. How should the court treat these sources?
o: The enacted text controls over a conflicting comment; the other state's decision is persuasive, not binding.
The comment controls, because the drafters' explanation is the best evidence of what the section means.
Both are binding, because the UCC requires uniform interpretation among the states.
Neither may be considered; the court may look only at the statutory text.
oe: Correct. Official Comments are the most important interpretive aid, but they aren't law and may be wrong where a state enacted non-uniform text. The UCC is a model; only the enacted version is law. Decisions from other states are persuasive because the Code aims at uniformity (§ 1-103(a)(3)).
A comment never overrides the enacted text, especially when the legislature departed from the uniform version.
Uniformity is a purpose that makes other states' cases persuasive. It doesn't make them binding authority.
Courts routinely consult comments, case law, treatises, and legislative history after reading the text.
topic: Wk 1 · The UCC & which law governs — Text versus comments

q: A court must interpret an ambiguous Article 2 provision. Section 1-103(a) directs that the UCC be liberally construed to promote its underlying purposes. Which of the following is NOT one of the purposes listed in § 1-103(a)?
o: To protect consumers from unfair commercial practices.
To simplify, clarify, and modernize the law governing commercial transactions.
To permit the continued expansion of commercial practices through custom, usage, and agreement.
To make uniform the law among the various jurisdictions.
oe: Correct. Consumer protection isn't among the listed purposes; consumer statutes are left in place by § 2-102(3)(b). The three purposes are to simplify, clarify, and modernize commercial law; to permit continued expansion of commercial practices through custom, usage, and agreement; and to make the law uniform among jurisdictions.
That is the first listed purpose.
That is the second listed purpose, and it is why trade usage and course of dealing carry so much weight.
That is the third listed purpose, which makes other states' decisions persuasive.
topic: Wk 1 · The UCC & which law governs — Purposes and themes

q: In January, a rancher signs a contract stating: “I hereby sell to Buyer the calves my herd will drop this spring.” In February, before any calves are born, the rancher's creditor claims the herd. Buyer argues that it already owns the unborn calves. Which statement is most accurate?
o: The calves are goods, but as future goods the “present sale” is only a contract to sell.
The calves aren't goods until they are born, so the contract is governed by the common law.
Buyer owns the calves outright, because the contract says “I hereby sell.”
The contract is void, because a seller can't sell goods that don't yet exist.
oe: Correct. “Goods” includes the unborn young of animals (§ 2-105(1)). Goods not both existing and identified are future goods, and a purported present sale of them operates as a contract to sell (§ 2-105(2)). Identification of unborn young occurs when they are conceived, if they are to be born within 12 months (§ 2-501).
Section 2-105(1) expressly includes the unborn young of animals within “goods.”
A present sale of future goods can't be accomplished by words alone; it operates as a contract to sell.
Contracts to sell future goods are valid. They simply can't operate as present sales.
topic: Wk 1 · The UCC & which law governs — Future goods

q: A toaster manufacturer asks its lawyer to draft standard sales terms. According to the course materials, which best describes the lawyer's principal job in drafting them?
o: Allocating risk: anticipating what can go wrong and drafting clear, enforceable terms for it.
Using formal legal phrasing so a court will recognize the terms as binding.
Restating the UCC's default rules so the customer can't claim surprise.
Preparing for litigation, since most sales contracts end up in dispute resolution.
oe: Correct. The transactional lawyer's main job is risk allocation, such as warranting the toaster is fit for ordinary purposes while limiting liability if a defect burns down a house. Good drafting means understanding the deal, knowing the rules and risk options, close attention to detail, and concise, clear language.
The materials stress avoiding legalese in favor of short, clear, active sentences.
Defaults apply without being restated. The value of drafting is deciding where to depart from them.
Disputes are the rare third stage of a deal; most of the work happens before and during performance.
topic: Wk 1 · The UCC & which law governs — The transactional lawyer's job

q: At a yard sale, Pat silently hands the seller $40, the price on a tag attached to a bicycle, and rides away. No one says a word. The bicycle turns out to have a cracked frame. Under the UCC's definitions, which statement is most accurate?
o: There is an “agreement” (a bargain in fact, inferred from conduct), and the “contract” is the total legal obligation the Code attaches to it.
There is no contract, because no one made a promise and the common law requires an exchange of promises or a promise for performance.
The agreement and the contract are the same thing: whatever the parties actually said or did.
There is a contract only if the price was $500 or more, because smaller sales are governed by the common law.
oe: Correct. An agreement is the bargain of the parties in fact, found in their language or inferred from circumstances (§ 1-201(b)(3)). The contract is the total legal obligation resulting from it under the UCC and other law (§ 1-201(b)(12)). The contract can be more than the agreement (gap fillers, implied terms) or less (unenforceable parts).
Article 2 is built on bargains, not promises. Conduct that shows agreement is enough (§ 2-204(1)).
The contract includes terms the law supplies, so it can differ from the parties' bargain in fact.
Price relates to the statute of frauds, not to whether there is an agreement or a contract.
topic: Wk 1 · Formation & the battle of the forms — Agreement vs. contract

q: Over several weeks of emails, a hospital and a supplier discuss buying 300 infusion pumps but never sign a document; the emails leave the delivery schedule and payment date unresolved. The supplier ships 100 pumps, the hospital uses them and pays, and the supplier ships 100 more. When the market price rises, the supplier refuses to ship the last 100, arguing there was never a contract because no one can say when it was formed and key terms were left open. What is the strongest response?
o: A contract exists: conduct can show agreement, even with open terms and no fixed moment of formation.
No contract exists, because an enforceable contract requires agreement on all material terms.
A contract exists, but only for the 200 pumps already shipped, because terms for the remainder were never agreed.
No contract exists, because Article 2 doesn't define “offer” and the emails therefore can't be an offer.
oe: Correct. Section 2-204 allows formation by conduct recognizing a contract (subsection (1)), doesn't require identifying the exact moment (subsection (2)), and lets open terms stand if the parties intended a contract and there is a reasonably certain basis for a remedy (subsection (3)). Gap fillers supply delivery and payment terms.
That is the common-law rule. Section 2-204(3) is a substantial departure from it.
The conduct recognizes a contract for the whole deal discussed. The question is intent plus a basis for a remedy, not agreement on every term.
Article 2 doesn't define offer, so the common law (Restatement § 24) does. That gap doesn't prevent formation.
topic: Wk 1 · Formation & the battle of the forms — Formation by conduct

q: A seller emails a merchant buyer an offer to sell 1,000 pallets. The email says nothing about how to accept. The buyer accepts by sending a signed letter by overnight courier, which arrives the next day. The seller argues that an emailed offer may be accepted only by email. What result?
o: Effective: absent an unambiguous requirement, any reasonable manner and medium may be used.
The acceptance is ineffective, because the offeror is the master of the offer and chose email.
The acceptance is effective only if the seller hadn't yet revoked, because a mailed acceptance is effective only on receipt.
The acceptance is ineffective, because Article 2 requires acceptances of offers over $500 to be in electronic form.
oe: Correct. Section 2-206(1)(a) abolishes the common-law presumption that acceptance must use the offer's medium. The offeror remains master of the offer, but must unambiguously require a particular manner.
Choosing a medium for the offer isn't an unambiguous requirement that acceptance use the same medium.
The question asks whether courier is a permitted medium; it is. Nothing suggests a revocation.
No such rule exists. Section 2-201 concerns enforceability, not the medium of acceptance.
topic: Wk 1 · Formation & the battle of the forms — Medium of acceptance

q: A buyer emails an order for 500 blue widgets “for prompt shipment.” The seller, out of blue, promptly ships 500 green widgets without saying anything. The buyer refuses them and sues for breach. The seller argues no contract was formed because it never accepted the buyer's offer for blue widgets. What result?
o: The shipment was both an acceptance and a breach, so the buyer may sue.
The shipment was a counter-offer, which the buyer rejected, so there is no contract.
The shipment was an acceptance, but there is no breach because the buyer could have accepted the green widgets.
No contract was formed, because a seller can accept only by a prompt promise to ship.
oe: Correct. Under § 2-206(1)(b), an offer to buy for prompt shipment may be accepted by prompt shipment of conforming or nonconforming goods. Shipping nonconforming goods without an accommodation notice creates a contract and breaches it at the same moment.
It would be a counter-offer only if the seller seasonably notified the buyer that the shipment was offered as an accommodation.
Green widgets don't conform to an order for blue widgets. The seller accepted and breached.
Section 2-206(1)(b) allows acceptance either by a prompt promise to ship or by prompt shipment.
topic: Wk 1 · Formation & the battle of the forms — Acceptance by shipment

q: Variation: When the seller ships the green widgets, it emails the buyer: “We're out of blue. We're sending green as an accommodation, in case they help you. Keep them at our list price or send them back at our expense.” The buyer rejects the green widgets and sues for breach. What result?
o: No breach: an accommodation shipment with notice is a counter-offer, not an acceptance.
Breach: any shipment in response to an order for prompt shipment is an acceptance.
Breach, because the notice came by email rather than in a signed writing.
No breach, but only because the buyer is required to accept a reasonable substitute.
oe: Correct. The accommodation proviso in § 2-206(1)(b) turns the nonconforming shipment into a counter-offer. The buyer may accept or reject it, but no contract for blue widgets was formed.
The statute carves out shipments that the seller seasonably labels as accommodations.
Section 2-206(1)(b) requires seasonable notice, not a signed writing.
Nothing requires the buyer to accept a substitute here. There's simply no contract for the blue widgets.
topic: Wk 1 · Formation & the battle of the forms — Accommodation shipment
pre: A buyer emails an order for 500 blue widgets “for prompt shipment.” The seller, out of blue, promptly ships 500 green widgets without saying anything. The buyer refuses them and sues for breach. The seller argues no contract was formed because it never accepted the buyer's offer for blue widgets. What result?

q: A buyer's offer to a fabricator invites acceptance by starting work on a custom steel stairway. The fabricator begins cutting steel the next day but tells no one. Five weeks later, having heard nothing, the buyer contracts with another fabricator and notifies the first that it's withdrawing the offer. Which statement best describes the buyer's position?
o: The buyer may treat the offer as lapsed, because it got no notice within a reasonable time.
The buyer is bound, because beginning performance completed the contract regardless of notice.
The buyer is bound, because offers inviting acceptance by performance are irrevocable once made.
The buyer may withdraw only by paying for the steel already cut.
oe: Correct. Under § 2-206(2), where beginning a requested performance is a reasonable mode of acceptance, an offeror who isn't notified of acceptance within a reasonable time may treat the offer as lapsed.
Beginning performance can accept, but § 2-206(2) protects an offeror who receives no notice within a reasonable time.
There is no such rule. Even a firm offer must meet § 2-205's requirements.
Section 2-206(2) lets the offeror treat the offer as lapsed; it doesn't condition that on reimbursing the offeree.
topic: Wk 1 · Formation & the battle of the forms — Notice of beginning performance

q: On March 1, a lumber yard emails a builder a signed quotation: “We will sell you 40 bundles of cedar at $900 per bundle. This offer will be held open until March 31.” The builder gave nothing in exchange. On March 14, after cedar prices jump, the yard emails: “Our quote is withdrawn.” On March 20, the builder emails its acceptance. Is there a contract?
o: Yes: a merchant's signed assurance to hold an offer open needs no consideration.
No: an offer can be made irrevocable only by consideration, and the builder gave none.
No: a firm offer binds only if both the offeror and the offeree are merchants.
Yes, but only because the builder's acceptance came within 30 days of the offer.
oe: Correct. Section 2-205 requires an offer by a merchant, in a signed record, that by its terms assures it will be held open. It is irrevocable for the stated time (or a reasonable time), never more than three months. The March 14 revocation was ineffective.
That is the common-law option rule. Section 2-205 dispenses with consideration for merchants' signed firm offers.
Only the offeror must be a merchant. The offeree's status doesn't matter.
The relevant period is the time stated in the offer (here, until March 31), capped at three months.
topic: Wk 1 · Formation & the battle of the forms — Firm offers

q: A buyer sends a supplier the buyer's own preprinted request-for-quote form. In it, the supplier fills in a price and signs at the bottom. The form's fine print, drafted by the buyer, says: “Supplier agrees this quote is irrevocable for six months.” Four months later, the supplier revokes before the buyer accepts. Which statement is most accurate?
o: Effective: the assurance on the offeree's form wasn't separately signed, and three months is the cap.
The revocation is ineffective: the supplier signed the form, so the six-month term binds it.
The revocation is ineffective for the first three months only, so it is effective now; the separate-signature rule doesn't matter.
The revocation is ineffective because the buyer, as offeree, drafted the assurance term in reliance on it.
oe: Correct. Section 2-205 requires that an assurance on a form supplied by the offeree be separately signed by the offeror. And even a proper firm offer is irrevocable for no more than three months without consideration.
A signature at the bottom of the offeree's form isn't the separate signature § 2-205 requires for the assurance term.
The three-month cap is one reason, but the missing separate signature means the assurance never bound the supplier at all.
Reliance by the offeree doesn't substitute for § 2-205's requirements.
topic: Wk 1 · Formation & the battle of the forms — Firm offer: time limits and forms

q: Over the phone, a merchant seller tells a manufacturer, “I'll hold this price on 2,000 brackets for you for 30 days.” Relying on that, the manufacturer spends $8,000 retooling its line. Ten days later the seller revokes. The offer didn't invite acceptance by performance. Which statement is most accurate?
o: The offer was revocable: an oral offer isn't a firm offer, and beginning preparation isn't acceptance.
The offer was irrevocable, because the seller is a merchant and stated a time.
The retooling accepted the offer, because the manufacturer began performance.
The offer was irrevocable for a reasonable time, because 30 days is within the three-month cap.
oe: Correct. A firm offer must be in a signed record (§ 2-205). Preparing to perform isn't acceptance unless the offer invited acceptance by performance (Problem 2-2 themes). The manufacturer might try promissory estoppel, but § 2-205 doesn't help.
Merchant status and a stated time aren't enough; § 2-205 requires a signed record.
Retooling is preparation, and the offer didn't invite acceptance by performance.
The cap limits proper firm offers. An oral offer never becomes a firm offer.
topic: Wk 1 · Formation & the battle of the forms — Firm offer: limits

q: A buyer's purchase order offers to buy a machine. The seller's acknowledgment form agrees to the quantity, price, and delivery date, but its boilerplate adds new terms and states: “Seller's acceptance is expressly limited to the terms of this acknowledgment.” The seller ships, and the buyer pays. Later the parties dispute which terms govern. In a court following Daitom v. Pennwalt, did the acknowledgment form a contract under § 2-207(1)?
o: Yes: boilerplate isn't enough; the offeree must clearly refuse to proceed without its terms.
No: any acknowledgment that adds terms is a counter-offer, which the buyer accepted by paying.
No: the seller's “expressly limited” language made its acceptance conditional, so § 2-207(3) governs.
Yes, but only because the seller's terms didn't materially alter the offer.
oe: Correct. Daitom followed Dorton v. Collins & Aikman. “Expressly conditional on assent” requires an explicit signal of unwillingness to proceed absent assent. Boilerplate didn't suffice, so the acknowledgment operated as an acceptance under § 2-207(1).
That is the common-law mirror-image and last-shot result § 2-207(1) was written to abolish.
Under Daitom and Dorton, this boilerplate doesn't make acceptance expressly conditional. Roto-Lith's contrary view is the minority.
Whether terms materially alter matters under § 2-207(2), not to whether a contract was formed under § 2-207(1).
topic: Wk 1 · Formation & the battle of the forms — Expressly conditional acceptance

q: A distributor's purchase order for 10,000 gaskets says nothing about warranties or interest. The manufacturer's acknowledgment accepts and adds two terms: (1) “Interest of 1.5% per month on overdue invoices,” which is standard in the trade, and (2) “Seller disclaims all implied warranties, including merchantability.” Both parties are merchants; the buyer doesn't respond, and the goods are delivered. Which terms became part of the contract?
o: Only the interest term; the disclaimer materially alters the contract and drops out.
Both: between merchants, additional terms become part of the contract unless the buyer objects.
Neither: additional terms in an acceptance are always mere proposals that require express assent.
Only the disclaimer, because warranty terms in a merchant's form are presumed accepted.
oe: Correct. Between merchants, additional terms become part of the contract unless the offer limits acceptance, they materially alter it, or there's timely objection (§ 2-207(2)). Comment 4 lists a clause negating standard warranties as a material alteration; comment 5 treats interest on overdue invoices within trade practice as not material.
Objection is only one exception. A term that materially alters the contract doesn't come in even without objection.
That's the rule for deals involving a non-merchant. Between merchants, non-material additional terms come in automatically.
A warranty disclaimer is the textbook material alteration, so it is the term that drops out.
topic: Wk 1 · Formation & the battle of the forms — Additional terms between merchants

q: Variation: The buyer's purchase order had stated: “Acceptance is limited to the terms of this order.” Everything else is the same. Does the interest term become part of the contract?
o: No: the offer's limitation keeps all additional terms out.
Yes, because the interest term is customary and not a material alteration.
Yes, unless the buyer objects in writing within ten days.
No, because the limiting clause means no contract was formed.
oe: Correct. Section 2-207(2)(a) keeps out additional terms when the offer expressly limits acceptance to its own terms, even if they are not material.
Non-materiality matters only if no exception applies. The offer's limitation independently excludes the term.
The ten-day period belongs to merchant confirmations under § 2-201(2), and objection is unnecessary when the offer limits acceptance.
The acknowledgment still accepted under § 2-207(1); the limiting clause only keeps the additional terms out.
topic: Wk 1 · Formation & the battle of the forms — Material alteration and objection
pre: A distributor's purchase order for 10,000 gaskets says nothing about warranties or interest. The manufacturer's acknowledgment accepts and adds two terms: (1) “Interest of 1.5% per month on overdue invoices,” which is standard in the trade, and (2) “Seller disclaims all implied warranties, including merchantability.” Both parties are merchants; the buyer doesn't respond, and the goods are delivered. Which terms became part of the contract?

q: A homeowner emails a furniture store an order for a $3,000 dining set. The store's emailed acceptance adds: “All disputes will be resolved by binding arbitration in the store's home county.” The homeowner never responds to that term, and the set is delivered and paid for. Is the arbitration clause part of the contract?
o: No: because the homeowner isn't a merchant, the additional term is only a proposal, and silence isn't assent.
Yes: additional terms become part of the contract unless the offeree objects within a reasonable time.
Yes, because arbitration clauses are favored by federal law.
No, because the store's acceptance with an added term was a counter-offer and no contract was formed.
oe: Correct. Section 2-207(2)'s automatic inclusion applies only between merchants. Otherwise additional terms are mere proposals for addition that require the other party's assent.
That describes the between-merchants rule, and it doesn't apply when one party is a consumer.
Federal arbitration policy doesn't decide whether a term was agreed to in the first place.
A contract was formed under § 2-207(1); only the additional term is excluded.
topic: Wk 1 · Formation & the battle of the forms — Non-merchant proposals

q: A buyer's purchase order says the buyer reserves “all rights and remedies available at law.” The seller's acceptance, a definite expression of acceptance, says “any action for breach must be brought within one year.” Both are merchants. Two and a half years after delivery, the buyer sues for breach of warranty. A court follows Daitom v. Pennwalt. Is the suit timely?
o: Yes: the conflicting terms knock each other out, and the gap filler, § 2-725's four-year limitations period, applies.
No: the seller's term was the last one sent before performance, so it controls.
No: different terms in an acceptance are treated as accepted between merchants unless objected to.
Yes, but only because the one-year term materially altered the offer and dropped out, leaving the buyer's terms.
oe: Correct. Daitom applied the knock-out rule to different (conflicting) terms: neither party's term governs, and the contract consists of the agreed terms plus Article 2's gap fillers, including the four-year period.
That's the common-law last-shot rule, which § 2-207 displaced.
Section 2-207(2) speaks only of additional terms. Under the preferred knock-out approach, conflicting terms cancel out.
That is a minority approach (the offeror's terms control). Daitom applied the knock-out rule and the gap filler.
topic: Wk 1 · Formation & the battle of the forms — Different terms: knock-out

q: A seller's response to a buyer's order states: “Our acceptance is expressly conditional on your assent to our terms, and we will not proceed otherwise.” The buyer never assents, but the seller ships, and the buyer accepts and uses the goods. The seller's terms included a strict limitation on remedies. What are the terms of the contract?
o: The terms on which the writings agree, plus Article 2's gap fillers.
The seller's terms, because the buyer accepted the goods knowing of the seller's conditions.
The buyer's terms, because the buyer made the offer and the offeror is master of the offer.
There is no contract, because the expressly conditional acceptance prevented formation.
oe: Correct. The response was expressly conditional, so the writings formed no contract under § 2-207(1). The parties' conduct did, under § 2-207(3), and its terms are those on which the writings agree plus supplementary terms supplied by the Code.
Accepting goods isn't assent to the seller's terms. Under § 2-207(3), neither side's unagreed terms control.
No contract was formed on the offer's terms. The § 2-207(3) contract includes only agreed terms plus gap fillers.
It prevented formation by the writings, but conduct recognizing a contract establishes one under § 2-207(3).
topic: Wk 1 · Formation & the battle of the forms — Contract by conduct

q: A buyer orders a $1,200 espresso machine on a seller's website. Above the “Place order” button is a clearly labeled link, “Terms of Sale,” which leads to a limitation of remedies. The buyer clicks “Place order” without opening the link. Later the buyer argues the limitation isn't part of the contract. What is the most likely result?
o: Likely yes: clearly labeled terms a reasonable buyer would notice are part of the deal.
The limitation isn't part of the contract, because the buyer never actually read it.
The limitation isn't part of the contract, because hyperlinked terms are always § 2-207 proposals.
The limitation is part of the contract only if the buyer is a merchant.
oe: Correct. Terms displayed where the buyer clicks to agree are part of the contract, and hyperlinked terms are too if a reasonable buyer would have been aware of them. Hidden, hard-to-access, or mislabeled links don't count.
Failing to read terms the buyer had a fair opportunity to see doesn't keep them out.
That is Klocek's view of terms shipped in the box, not of clearly presented terms before purchase.
The reasonable-awareness test applies to consumers as well; merchant status matters to § 2-207(2), not here.
topic: Wk 1 · Formation & the battle of the forms — Online terms

q: Which of the following is NOT one of the ways Article 2 changes the common law of offer and acceptance?
o: It requires that every acceptance mirror the offer's material terms.
It allows a seller to accept an order by promptly shipping goods.
It makes a merchant's signed firm offer irrevocable without consideration.
It allows a written confirmation to operate as an acceptance.
oe: Correct. That's the common-law mirror-image rule, which § 2-207(1) abolishes. Article 2's changes include: acceptance by any reasonable medium (§ 2-206(1)(a)); acceptance by shipping goods (§ 2-206(1)(b)); firm offers without consideration (§ 2-205); and treating a confirmation as an acceptance (§ 2-207(1)).
That is § 2-205.
That is § 2-207(1), the “staggering alchemy” the text describes.
topic: Wk 1 · Formation & the battle of the forms — Common law vs. UCC formation

q: After a phone call, a grower emails a restaurant group: “Confirming you'll buy our heirloom tomatoes this season. — Ana Ruiz, Ruiz Farms.” The email names no quantity and no price. When prices rise, Ruiz Farms refuses to deliver, and the restaurant group sues for 5,000 pounds at $2 per pound. Ruiz Farms raises the statute of frauds. What result?
o: Insufficient: the record states no quantity, so nothing is enforceable.
The record is insufficient, because it omits the price, which is an essential term of any sale.
The record is sufficient, because it is signed by the party to be charged and indicates a contract.
The statute of frauds doesn't apply, because the restaurant group is the one seeking enforcement.
oe: Correct. A § 2-201(1) record must indicate a contract for sale, be signed by the party to be charged, and state a quantity. Price and other terms may be omitted or misstated, but quantity is essential.
Price can be omitted; the statute says a record isn't insufficient because it omits a term agreed upon. Quantity is the exception.
Those are two of the three requirements. The contract isn't enforceable beyond the quantity shown, and here none is shown.
Section 2-201 protects the party against whom enforcement is sought, here Ruiz Farms. Who sues doesn't make the statute inapplicable.
topic: Wks 1–2 · Statute of frauds & unconscionability — The record's contents

q: A buyer orally agrees to buy 20 used copiers from a dealer for $14,000. The buyer then emails the dealer: “Per our call, we're buying 20 copiers at $700 each. Thanks! — Jordan Lee, Purchasing.” The dealer never replies or signs anything. Assume the buyer isn't a merchant. Later the buyer sues the dealer for refusing to deliver. Can the buyer enforce the deal against the dealer?
o: No: the record must be signed by the party against whom enforcement is sought, and the dealer signed nothing.
Yes: a typed name in an email is a signature, so the record satisfies § 2-201 against either party.
No: an email can never be a signed writing under the statute of frauds.
Yes: both parties must sign only when the price exceeds $5,000.
oe: Correct. Jordan's typed name is almost certainly a signature, but it binds only the buyer. The dealer, the party to be charged, signed no record, and nothing shows that both parties are merchants, so the confirmation exception isn't available.
A record satisfies § 2-201(1) only against the party who signed it. Here that is the buyer, not the dealer.
After the 2022 amendments (and under UETA), an email is a record, and a typed name with intent to adopt it is a signature.
There is no two-signature rule. And the $5,000 threshold appeared only in the withdrawn 2003 amendments.
topic: Wks 1–2 · Statute of frauds & unconscionability — Signed by the party to be charged

q: Variation: The buyer is a business that regularly buys office equipment, so both parties are merchants. The dealer receives Jordan's email, reads it, and says nothing for three weeks. Can the buyer now overcome the dealer's statute of frauds defense?
o: Yes: a proper merchant confirmation binds a merchant who doesn't object in writing within ten days.
No: the dealer still never signed anything, and silence can't satisfy the statute of frauds.
Yes, and the buyer automatically wins the case, because the dealer lost the right to dispute the contract.
No: the dealer had 30 days to object, and only three weeks passed.
oe: Correct. All the § 2-201(2) elements are met: oral agreement between merchants, a confirmation sent within a reasonable time, sufficient against the sender (signed, indicates a contract, states a quantity), received with reason to know its contents, and no written objection within ten days.
Between merchants, silence after receiving a proper confirmation does exactly that. “Merchants must read their mail.”
The confirmation only removes the statute of frauds defense. The buyer must still prove that the contract was made and its terms.
The objection period is ten days after receipt, not 30.
topic: Wks 1–2 · Statute of frauds & unconscionability — Merchant confirmations
pre: A buyer orally agrees to buy 20 used copiers from a dealer for $14,000. The buyer then emails the dealer: “Per our call, we're buying 20 copiers at $700 each. Thanks! — Jordan Lee, Purchasing.” The dealer never replies or signs anything. Assume the buyer isn't a merchant. Later the buyer sues the dealer for refusing to deliver. Can the buyer enforce the deal against the dealer?

q: After a phone negotiation, a merchant seller sends a merchant buyer a signed note: “Thanks for your interest in our widgets. We'd be happy to quote you on whatever quantity you need.” The buyer receives it and doesn't object for 30 days. The seller then sues the buyer for refusing to take 500 widgets. Does § 2-201(2) defeat the buyer's statute of frauds defense?
o: No: the note doesn't indicate a contract or state a quantity, so it wouldn't bind the sender.
Yes: the buyer received a signed writing and didn't object within ten days.
Yes: the note's reference to widgets is enough, because the quantity can be proved by oral testimony.
No, but only because the seller waited 30 days to sue.
oe: Correct. A confirmation must be a record that would satisfy § 2-201(1) if the sender were the defendant: signed by the sender, indicating a contract for sale, and stating a quantity. A note offering a quote does none of that, so the recipient's silence doesn't matter (Problem 2-10(A)).
Silence matters only if the confirmation would bind the sender. The sender can't bind the recipient with a document that wouldn't bind itself.
A record isn't enforceable beyond the quantity it shows. Oral testimony can't supply a missing quantity.
Timing of the lawsuit isn't the issue; the note simply isn't a confirmation of a contract.
topic: Wks 1–2 · Statute of frauds & unconscionability — Sufficient against the sender

q: Silas, a merchant buyer, receives a merchant seller's proper written confirmation of an oral deal for 1,000 units, including a term “payment due in 90 days.” Five days later, Silas emails: “I never agreed to payment in 90 days. Payment is due in 30.” The seller later sues on the contract. Can the seller use § 2-201(2) to defeat Silas's statute of frauds defense?
o: No: Silas gave written notice of objection to the confirmation's contents within ten days of receipt.
Yes: Silas objected only to the payment term, so the rest of the confirmation binds him.
Yes: an objection must be sent by mail, so an email doesn't count.
No: § 2-201(2) applies only when the seller sends the confirmation to a consumer.
oe: Correct. A written objection within ten days defeats the merchant's confirmation exception (Problem 2-10(B)). The seller must find another way to satisfy the statute, such as an admission or part performance.
The statute asks whether the recipient objected to the confirmation's contents. Objecting to its contents within ten days defeats § 2-201(2).
An email is a record, and the objection need only be written notice.
The confirmation exception applies only between merchants, as here.
topic: Wks 1–2 · Statute of frauds & unconscionability — Written objection

q: After a phone call, a fabricator begins making 50,000 custom circuit boards printed with a buyer's logo and built to the buyer's unique specs. It has completed 12,000 and ordered parts for 20,000 more when the buyer calls to cancel. There is no signed record. In the fabricator's suit, which statement is most accurate?
o: Enforceable under the specially-manufactured-goods exception, at least for boards begun or committed.
The contract is unenforceable, because there's no signed record and the price exceeds $500.
The contract is enforceable only if the fabricator finished all 50,000 boards before the cancellation.
The contract is enforceable for all 50,000 boards, because the buyer's repudiation waived the statute of frauds.
oe: Correct. Section 2-201(3)(a) applies to goods specially manufactured for the buyer, not suitable for sale to others in the seller's ordinary course, where the seller made a substantial beginning or commitments before notice of repudiation. Whether it reaches the full 50,000 is debated (Problem 2-11).
An exception applies. That's the point of § 2-201(3)(a).
The exception requires a substantial beginning of manufacture or commitments for procurement, not completion.
Repudiation doesn't waive the statute; the exception protects only the seller's reliance before notice of repudiation, and its reach beyond that is uncertain.
topic: Wks 1–2 · Statute of frauds & unconscionability — Specially manufactured goods

q: A buyer sues a seller on an oral contract for 300 bicycles. There's no signed record. In its answer, the seller denies any contract, but at deposition the seller's president testifies: “We did agree to sell them 100 bikes, but never 300.” What is the most the buyer can enforce?
o: A contract for 100 bicycles, the quantity admitted.
A contract for 300 bicycles, because the admission removes the statute of frauds defense entirely.
Nothing, because the seller's answer denied the contract.
Nothing, because admissions count only if they're in the defendant's pleading.
oe: Correct. Under § 2-201(3)(b), a contract is enforceable if the party against whom enforcement is sought admits in pleading, testimony, or otherwise in court that a contract was made, but not beyond the quantity admitted.
The admission exception is limited to the quantity of goods admitted.
The admission can come in testimony as well as pleadings. The deposition testimony counts.
The statute covers admissions in pleading, testimony, or otherwise in court.
topic: Wks 1–2 · Statute of frauds & unconscionability — Admission

q: A buyer sues on an alleged oral contract to buy a custom sailboat. There's no signed record, and the seller moves to dismiss under § 2-201. The buyer argues dismissal is premature because the seller might admit the contract in discovery, and alternatively that promissory estoppel avoids the statute. Under Casazza v. Kiser, how should the court rule?
o: Grant it: a hoped-for admission isn't enough, and promissory estoppel didn't apply here.
Deny the motion: a plaintiff is always entitled to discovery to try to obtain an admission.
Deny the motion: promissory estoppel always overcomes the statute of frauds in a sale of goods.
Grant the motion only if the boat cost more than $5,000.
oe: Correct. Casazza held a plaintiff's hope that the defendant will admit the contract is not enough. It also found promissory estoppel unavailable under all three approaches: the Restatement view (a promise to put the deal in writing), the restrictive view (never), and the least restrictive view (only to prevent fraud or unconscionable injury).
Casazza rejected that argument; a speculative future admission doesn't keep the claim alive.
Courts take three approaches, and the most restrictive never allows it. Casazza found it unavailable under all three.
The threshold is $500.
topic: Wks 1–2 · Statute of frauds & unconscionability — Hoped-for admission

q: Under an oral deal, a buyer agreed to buy a $300,000 sailboat and, separately, its $4,000 navigation software package. The seller delivered the software, and the buyer accepted and paid for it. When the seller refuses to deliver the boat, the buyer argues that part performance satisfies the statute of frauds for the whole deal. Under Casazza v. Kiser, what result?
o: Unenforceable: part performance covers only the software, a separate commercial unit.
The whole deal is enforceable, because any part performance takes an oral contract out of the statute.
The whole deal is enforceable, because the software was paid for in full.
Nothing is enforceable, including the software, because the statute applies to the whole transaction.
oe: Correct. Section 2-201(3)(c) makes a contract enforceable only as to goods paid for and accepted or received and accepted. Casazza held that accepting the software wasn't part performance of the boat contract, because they weren't one commercial unit (§ 2-105(6)).
Article 2's part-performance exception is limited to the goods actually paid for and accepted, or received and accepted.
Payment for the software reaches only the software.
The software was paid for and accepted, so the contract is enforceable as to it.
topic: Wks 1–2 · Statute of frauds & unconscionability — Part performance and commercial units

q: A seller sues for breach and produces two documents: an unsigned purchase order listing “200 drums of solvent,” and the buyer's signed letter that refers to “our order of March 3 for solvent” and asks to delay delivery. The court finds the statute of frauds satisfied. What follows?
o: The seller may proceed, but it still must prove the contract existed, its terms, and the breach.
The seller wins, because a writing satisfying § 2-201 is conclusive proof of the contract.
The court erred, because separate documents can never be combined to satisfy the statute of frauds.
The seller may proceed, but only for the quantity in the buyer's signed letter, which doesn't state one.
oe: Correct. Writings that refer to one another can be read together to satisfy § 2-201 (Casazza). But meeting the statute only opens the courthouse door; it doesn't prove the contract.
Satisfying the statute is a threshold, not proof of the deal's existence or terms.
Papers may be read together if they refer to one another or are connected by internal evidence.
Read together, the documents supply the quantity of 200 drums, and the buyer's letter supplies the signature.
topic: Wks 1–2 · Statute of frauds & unconscionability — Effect of satisfying the SOF

q: A furniture store sells a refrigerator on credit to a buyer who reads little English. Its preprinted contract, in small type and drafted in complex legalese, sets a price about three times the refrigerator's retail value. Two years later, after the buyer loses her job, she claims the contract is unconscionable. Which statement is most accurate?
o: The court decides, as of contracting, and may refuse enforcement, strike the clause, or limit it.
The jury decides whether the contract is unconscionable in light of the buyer's later job loss.
The contract can be unconscionable only if the buyer proves the store committed fraud.
The court may only refuse to enforce the entire contract; it can't strike or limit a single clause.
oe: Correct. Under § 2-302, unconscionability is measured at the time of contracting, is for the court, and allows the court to refuse enforcement, sever the clause, or limit its application. Here there are both procedural (language barrier, fine print) and substantive (inflated price) elements, as in Williams v. Walker-Thomas.
Unconscionability is a question of law for the court, and later changes in circumstances don't count.
Fraud is a separate doctrine. Unconscionability rests on oppression and unfair surprise.
Section 2-302(1) gives the court all three options.
topic: Wks 1–2 · Statute of frauds & unconscionability — Unconscionability

q: Two sophisticated companies negotiate for weeks, with counsel, over a contract for industrial parts. The final contract includes a price that turns out to be far above what other suppliers charge. The buyer later claims unconscionability. What is the buyer's biggest obstacle?
o: There's no procedural unconscionability, and many courts require both procedural and substantive elements.
Unconscionability applies only to consumer contracts, so a business buyer can never invoke it.
Price can never be an unconscionable term, because parties are free to set any price.
The buyer had to raise unconscionability before signing, or it is waived.
oe: Correct. Unconscionability has a procedural element (unfair surprise in the bargaining process) and a substantive one (oppressive, one-sided terms). Many courts require both; others use a sliding scale. Lengthy negotiation with counsel undercuts any claim of unfair surprise.
Most successful claims are consumer cases, but § 2-302 isn't limited to consumers.
An excessive price can be substantively unconscionable; Williams v. Walker-Thomas involved inflated prices.
There's no such rule. Section 2-302 also can't be varied by agreement.
topic: Wks 1–2 · Statute of frauds & unconscionability — Procedural and substantive

q: A 12-month contract calls for monthly deliveries “by the 5th.” The first delivery arrives on the 7th, and the buyer accepts it without comment. The seller now argues that a course of performance has established that delivery by the 7th is acceptable. Is the seller right?
o: No: a single occasion of conduct doesn't create a course of performance.
Yes: acceptance without objection of any late delivery changes the delivery term going forward.
Yes, because course of performance overrides express terms when the two conflict.
No, because course of performance can arise only from conduct before the contract was signed.
oe: Correct. A course of performance requires repeated occasions for performance, with the other party's knowledge and opportunity to object, and its acceptance or acquiescence (§ 1-303(a)). One late delivery isn't enough (Problem 3-5(A)).
Acquiescence in one occasion isn't a course of performance, and acceptance alone doesn't waive the buyer's claims (§ 2-607(2)).
Express terms prevail over course of performance when the two can't reasonably be reconciled (§ 1-303(e)).
Pre-contract conduct is course of dealing. Course of performance is conduct under the current contract.
topic: Wk 2 · Trade usage, dealing & good faith — Course of performance

q: A signed contract for a skid loader is silent about where delivery will take place. In five earlier purchases between the same parties, the seller always delivered equipment to the buyer's lot. The seller now insists the buyer pick up the loader at the seller's yard. What is the delivery term?
o: Delivery at the buyer's lot: the course of dealing leaves no gap for § 2-308.
Pickup at the seller's yard, because § 2-308 makes the seller's place of business the place of delivery.
Pickup at the seller's yard, because prior contracts can't vary the terms of a later signed contract.
Delivery at the buyer's lot, but only if the earlier contracts expressly required it.
oe: Correct. A course of dealing is a sequence of conduct in previous transactions between the parties that establishes a common basis of understanding (§ 1-303(b)). It's part of the agreement (§ 1-201(b)(3)), so the § 2-308 default never applies (Problem 3-8(B)).
Section 2-308 is a gap filler. It applies only if the agreement, including course of dealing, doesn't address delivery.
Course of dealing supplements and gives meaning to the parties' agreement; the contract here is silent, so nothing contradicts it.
Course of dealing is shown by conduct. The earlier contracts needn't have said so expressly.
topic: Wk 2 · Trade usage, dealing & good faith — Course of dealing fills a gap

q: A contract for asphalt between a paving contractor and a supplier sets a fixed price. The contractor offers evidence that in the local paving trade, suppliers always “price-protect” contractors by holding the old price for tonnage already committed to jobs when prices rise. The supplier objects that the practice isn't universal and dates back only ten years. Is the usage evidence admissible?
o: Likely yes, if proved as a regular trade practice and the contractor gave notice.
No, because a usage must be universal in the trade to be binding.
No, because any trade usage contradicts the express fixed-price term and is excluded.
Yes, automatically, because usage of trade is always part of every contract without proof.
oe: Correct. A usage of trade needs only such regularity of observance in a place, vocation, or trade as to justify an expectation it will be observed (§ 1-303(c)). It needn't be ancient, immemorial, or universal (cmt. 4). The offering party must give notice (§ 1-303(g)).
Comment 4 rejects requirements that a usage be universal or ancient.
Courts first try to construe express terms and usage consistently. Price protection arguably supplements the fixed price rather than contradicting it.
Usage must be proved as a fact by the party relying on it, and notice is required.
topic: Wk 2 · Trade usage, dealing & good faith — Usage of trade

q: A contract requires delivery “in steel drums.” For eight months, the seller delivered in plastic drums, and the buyer accepted them without objection. Industry usage is to deliver this chemical in plastic. The buyer now insists on steel. If the express term can't reasonably be reconciled with the conduct and usage, which controls?
o: The express term, which outranks course of performance, dealing, and usage.
Usage of trade, because it reflects the expectations of everyone in the industry.
Course of performance, because it's the most recent evidence of what the parties intended.
None of them; the court fills the gap with a reasonable term.
oe: Correct. Section 1-303(e) requires construing express terms and course of performance, course of dealing, and usage consistently where reasonable; if that's unreasonable, express terms control. (Course of performance may still show a waiver or modification, § 1-303(f).)
Usage of trade sits at the bottom of the hierarchy.
Course of performance outranks dealing and usage, but not express terms.
There's no gap; the parties expressly agreed on steel drums.
topic: Wk 2 · Trade usage, dealing & good faith — The hierarchy

q: A seller's form says: “This agreement shall not be affected by any usage of trade.” A buyer later offers evidence of a specific trade usage allowing a 2% shortage in grain shipments. What effect does the seller's clause most likely have?
o: Little: negating a usage generally requires identifying it specifically.
It bars the evidence completely, because parties may vary the effect of any Code provision by agreement.
It bars the evidence only if both parties are merchants.
It's void, because usage of trade can never be excluded by agreement.
oe: Correct. Usages are taken for granted unless carefully negated (§ 2-202 cmt. 2), and the text suggests a general clause purporting to exclude all usages is likely ineffective (Problem 3-1).
Freedom of contract allows negating a usage, but the materials suggest it must be done specifically.
Merchant status isn't the issue; the question is whether the clause negated the usage carefully enough.
Usages can be excluded; it simply takes specific language.
topic: Wk 2 · Trade usage, dealing & good faith — Negating a usage

q: In a state that has adopted revised Article 1's definition of good faith, a non-merchant seller performing a contract honestly believes it is entitled to delay delivery but acts in a way that departs from reasonable commercial standards of fair dealing. Has the seller satisfied the obligation of good faith?
o: No: revised Article 1 requires honesty plus fair dealing from everyone.
Yes: honest belief is all good faith requires.
Yes: the objective prong applies only to merchants, and this seller isn't one.
No: good faith requires a party to act as a fiduciary for the other party.
oe: Correct. Section 1-201(b)(20) has a subjective prong (honesty in fact) and an objective prong (reasonable commercial standards of fair dealing). In states that kept the old subjective-only Article 1 definition, a non-merchant would be held only to honesty in fact.
That was the old Article 1 standard. Revised Article 1 adds an objective prong for all parties.
That was true under former Article 2's merchant definition. Revised Article 1 extends the objective prong to non-merchants.
Good faith lies between a fiduciary duty and a mere duty to refrain from fraud (Market Street).
topic: Wk 2 · Trade usage, dealing & good faith — Defining good faith

q: A buyer sues a seller in a single count titled “Breach of the Duty of Good Faith Under § 1-304,” alleging the seller's conduct was unfair, without tying it to any contract term. The contract expressly lets the seller choose the shipping carrier. Which statement is most accurate?
o: It fails: § 1-304 isn't a stand-alone claim and can't override express terms.
The claim succeeds if the seller's conduct was unfair, because every contract imposes good faith.
The claim fails, because the contract implicitly disclaimed the duty of good faith by giving the seller discretion.
The claim succeeds, because good faith overrides any express term that operates unfairly.
oe: Correct. A failure to perform a specific contractual duty in good faith is a breach of that duty; there's no free-standing good-faith claim (§ 1-304 cmt. 1). Good faith is a lens for interpreting the agreement and shouldn't contradict express terms.
Good faith attaches to the performance of contractual duties; it isn't a stand-alone claim.
Good faith can't be disclaimed (§ 1-302(b)). The claim fails for other reasons.
Good faith shouldn't be used to contradict express terms.
topic: Wk 2 · Trade usage, dealing & good faith — No stand-alone claim

q: A supply contract states: (1) “Buyer waives any obligation of Seller to act in good faith,” and (2) “Seller will be deemed to act in good faith in setting delivery dates if it gives Buyer at least five business days' notice.” Which clauses are enforceable?
o: Only clause (2), if the standard isn't manifestly unreasonable.
Both, because parties may vary the effect of any UCC provision by agreement.
Neither, because the parties can't address good faith in their contract at all.
Only clause (1), because the buyer is entitled to waive protections that exist for its benefit.
oe: Correct. The obligation of good faith may not be disclaimed by agreement, but the parties may set standards for measuring performance if those standards aren't manifestly unreasonable (§ 1-302(b)).
Section 1-302(b) expressly bars disclaiming good faith, diligence, reasonableness, and care.
They can define how good faith is measured, within the manifestly-unreasonable limit.
A waiver of good faith is precisely what § 1-302(b) forbids.
topic: Wk 2 · Trade usage, dealing & good faith — Disclaiming vs. measuring

q: During negotiations, a seller of used industrial presses knows the market for presses is about to rise but says nothing, and the buyer agrees to a fixed price. The buyer later sues, claiming the seller breached the UCC's duty of good faith by failing to disclose its market forecast. What result?
o: It likely fails: § 1-304 covers performance and enforcement, not negotiations.
The claim succeeds, because good faith requires disclosing all material information before contracting.
The claim succeeds, because the seller is a merchant and merchants owe a heightened duty in negotiations.
The claim fails only because good faith in § 2-403 concerns good-faith purchasers, not sellers.
oe: Correct. Section 1-304 imposes good faith in the performance and enforcement of a contract. Before contracting, a party may generally exploit superior knowledge (Market Street). Separately, an isolated non-merchant seller must disclose known material hidden defects (§ 2-314 cmt. 3), which isn't this case.
Good faith doesn't reach formation, and there's no general duty to share market forecasts.
Merchant status doesn't extend the § 1-304 duty to negotiations.
The good-faith-purchaser concept in § 2-403 is a different idea. The claim fails because § 1-304 doesn't apply to negotiations.
topic: Wk 2 · Trade usage, dealing & good faith — Good faith and negotiations

q: A tenant's lease gives it the right to ask the landlord for financing for improvements; if the landlord refuses, the tenant may buy the property at a below-market price. The tenant's manager, knowing the landlord has forgotten this clause, sends a financing request that doesn't mention it, hoping for a refusal that will trigger the cheap purchase option. Under Market Street Associates v. Frey, is this consistent with good faith?
o: No: exploiting the other side's known oversight during performance is bad faith.
Yes: parties may exploit superior knowledge at any stage, because there's no duty to protect the other side.
No: a party to a contract owes the other party fiduciary duties of full disclosure.
Yes: good faith can never override an express contract term like the purchase option.
oe: Correct. Judge Posner described good faith as between a fiduciary duty and the duty merely to refrain from fraud. Exploiting a known oversight during performance crosses the line (and on remand, Market Street was found to have breached).
That freedom exists before contracting. After contracting, deliberate exploitation of an oversight is bad faith.
Market Street rejected a fiduciary standard; good faith is a narrower duty.
The option is enforceable in principle; the problem is the deliberately misleading way it was triggered.
topic: Wk 2 · Trade usage, dealing & good faith — Exploiting an oversight

q: Strawberry Computer's master agreement prices each Better Buy order at 80% of Strawberry's suggested retail price “on the day the order is accepted.” Strawberry decides to cut its retail price by 30%, waits until Better Buy places its large mid-month order, accepts it immediately at the old price, and announces the price cut the next day. Which is Better Buy's strongest argument, and Strawberry's best response?
o: Better Buy: opportunistic timing breached good faith. Strawberry: the price term is express.
Better Buy: the contract is unconscionable. Strawberry: Better Buy is a merchant and can't claim unconscionability.
Better Buy: good faith is an independent tort claim. Strawberry: torts aren't covered by the UCC.
Better Buy: the price term is void for indefiniteness. Strawberry: the term was agreed.
oe: Correct. Problem 3-2 pits Market Street (opportunism during an ongoing relationship) against Vintage Rodeo (no gap for good faith to fill where an express term governs). Better Buy could have protected itself with price-protection credits, advance notice of price changes, return rights, or most-favored-customer pricing.
Unconscionability is judged at contracting and doesn't fit post-contract timing tactics; merchants can raise it in any event.
Good faith isn't a stand-alone claim; the argument must be that Strawberry performed a contract duty in bad faith.
A price tied to a published retail price on a specified date is definite.
topic: Wk 2 · Trade usage, dealing & good faith — Express terms and opportunism

q: A seller agreed to deliver 5,000 bags of fertilizer at $20 each. A storm then destroyed a key supplier's plant, and the seller's costs rose so that it would lose money on every bag. The seller asks for $23 per bag, explaining the situation, and the buyer agrees in a signed email. Later the buyer refuses to pay more than $20, arguing it received no consideration for the increase. What result?
o: The modification is binding: it needs no consideration, and a cost increase making performance a loss is a legitimate commercial reason.
The modification is unenforceable under the pre-existing duty rule, because the seller was already obligated to deliver at $20.
The modification is enforceable only if it was fair and equitable in light of unanticipated circumstances under Restatement § 89.
The modification is unenforceable because the storm wouldn't qualify as impracticability under § 2-615.
oe: Correct. Section 2-209(1) dispenses with consideration for modifications, which are instead policed by good faith. Comment 2 says a market shift that makes performance involve a loss can justify seeking a modification, even if it wouldn't excuse performance.
That's the traditional common-law rule, which § 2-209(1) displaces.
Section 89 is the modern common-law rule. Article 2 is more lenient; it requires good faith, not § 89's test.
Comment 2 says a modification may be sought in good faith even when the circumstances wouldn't amount to legal excuse.
topic: Wk 2 · Modification, waiver & estoppel — No consideration needed

q: A steel mill agreed to sell steel at a fixed price for a year. When the market boomed, the mill told the buyer it would ship no steel at all for the rest of the year unless the buyer agreed to higher prices; it offered no contractual justification at the time. The buyer, unable to buy elsewhere, agreed. Assume the mill was in fact losing money. Under Roth Steel v. Sharon Steel, is the modification enforceable?
o: No: the threat to stop shipping showed a lack of honesty in fact that wasn't rebutted.
Yes: because the mill was losing money, it had a legitimate commercial reason, which is all good faith requires.
Yes: modifications need no consideration, so the buyer's agreement binds it regardless of how it was obtained.
No: a seller may seek a price increase only if performance has become commercially impracticable.
oe: Correct. Roth Steel's two-part test asks (1) whether a factor like increased costs would cause an ordinary merchant to seek a modification (objective), and (2) whether the party was actually motivated by a legitimate reason without coercion (subjective, honesty in fact). Sharon passed the first part and failed the second.
A legitimate reason satisfies only the objective prong. Coercive means can show a lack of honesty in fact.
No consideration is needed, but the modification still must be sought in good faith (§ 2-209 cmt. 2).
Roth Steel didn't require impracticability. And Man Industries rejected even the requirement that a seller face a loss.
topic: Wk 2 · Modification, waiver & estoppel — Roth Steel

q: A furniture dealer sells a $4,000 sectional sofa to a consumer on the dealer's own preprinted form, which the consumer signs at the bottom. Paragraph 12 of the fine print says: “This agreement may be modified only by a writing signed by both parties.” The dealer's salesperson later orally agrees to extend the delivery date, and the consumer relies on it. The dealer argues the oral modification is barred. Is it?
o: No: on a merchant's form, the consumer must separately sign the NOM clause.
Yes: a signed agreement excluding oral modification can't be otherwise modified.
Yes: NOM clauses are enforceable against anyone who signs the contract.
No: NOM clauses are never enforceable, because parties can always orally waive a writing requirement.
