o: Likely not: the default place is the seller's place of business.
Yes: the seller may tender wherever the goods happen to be stored.
Yes, because the buyer is responsible for transportation costs.
No, because the default place of delivery is the buyer's place of business.
oe: Correct. Section 2-308(a) makes the seller's place of business the default; § 2-308(b) applies only to identified goods that both parties knew at contracting were elsewhere (Problem 4-4(a)(4)).
Only if both parties knew at contracting that identified goods were there.
Who pays for transport doesn't change the place of tender.
The default is the seller's place of business.
topic: Wks 4–5 · Tender, delivery & payment — Place of delivery

q: Same wheat contract. The seller properly tenders all 100 bushels at its place of business. The buyer arrives with a small truck and asks to take half now and half the next afternoon. The seller refuses and demands full payment now. Who is right?
o: The seller: delivery is in one lot, and the buyer supplies facilities.
The buyer: a buyer may take goods in reasonable installments.
The buyer, because the seller must hold goods for a reasonable time.
Neither: the buyer must pay half now and half on the second pickup.
oe: Correct. Section 2-307 presumes a single lot, and § 2-503(1)(b) puts the facilities burden on the buyer. The buyer has no right to take in lots (Problem 4-4(a)(5)).
The default is a single delivery; lots require agreement.
The seller is holding them; the issue is the buyer's lack of facilities.
Payment is due on tender of the full single lot.
topic: Wks 4–5 · Tender, delivery & payment — Buyer's small truck

q: The parties agreed the seller would deliver 100 bushels to the buyer's farm on April 3. The seller arrives at a reasonable hour with conforming wheat, but the buyer's storage bin hasn't been cleaned out, and the buyer asks the seller to come back in two hours. Which statement is most accurate?
o: Proper tender; the buyer's failure to cooperate excuses the seller's delay.
The seller's tender was defective, because the buyer couldn't take delivery.
The seller must wait as long as the buyer needs without any remedy.
The contract is discharged, because performance became impossible.
oe: Correct. Under § 2-503(1)(b), the buyer furnishes facilities for receipt. Section 2-311(3) excuses the cooperating party's delay and lets it proceed reasonably (wait, charge for the delay) or treat a material failure as breach (Problem 4-4(a)(6)).
Tender requires the seller to make goods available; furnishing facilities is the buyer's obligation.
Section 2-311(3) gives the seller remedies for the buyer's failure to cooperate.
A two-hour delay in cleaning a bin isn't impossibility.
topic: Wks 4–5 · Tender, delivery & payment — Buyer not ready

q: On delivery, the buyer hands the seller a business check, which is the normal way payment is made in the trade. The seller insists on cash. The next day, the check bounces. Which statement is most accurate?
o: Payment by check was sufficient, but the bounced check revives the debt.
The buyer's tender was ineffective, because payment must be in cash unless the contract says otherwise.
Once the seller took the check, the buyer's payment obligation was discharged regardless of dishonor.
The seller may refuse any form of payment other than a certified check.
oe: Correct. Section 2-511(2) allows payment by any means current in the ordinary course of business unless the seller demands legal tender and gives a reasonable extension. Section 2-511(3) makes check payment conditional; dishonor defeats it as between the parties.
Any commercially current means works, subject to the legal-tender demand.
Check payment is conditional; dishonor revives the obligation.
The seller can demand legal tender (cash), not a particular form like a certified check.
topic: Wks 4–5 · Tender, delivery & payment — Payment by check

q: A farmer agrees to trade 40 hogs to a neighbor in exchange for the neighbor's used tractor. The tractor turns out to have a cracked engine block. Does Article 2 govern the farmer's claim about the tractor?
o: Yes: the price may be paid in goods, making each party a seller.
No: a barter isn't a sale, because no money changes hands.
No: only the party who receives money is a seller.
Yes, but only the farmer is a seller; the neighbor is merely a buyer.
oe: Correct. Section 2-304(1) allows the price to be paid in goods, realty, or services. In a goods-for-goods barter, each party is a seller of the goods it transfers. (If paid partly in realty, Article 2 governs only the goods side.)
Article 2 defines price broadly enough to include goods.
When the price is paid in goods, each party is a seller of what it transfers.
Both are sellers of the goods they transfer.
topic: Wks 4–5 · Tender, delivery & payment — Price paid in kind

q: A seller delivers 500 crates of produce on May 1. The contract says nothing about when payment is due. The buyer accepts the goods and says it will pay in 30 days, as its other suppliers allow. When is payment due?
o: On receipt, because credit isn't presumed.
Within 30 days, because that's a reasonable time for payment in commercial sales.
Within 30 days, because the buyer's other suppliers' practice is binding usage of trade.
Only after the buyer resells the produce.
oe: Correct. Section 2-310(a) makes payment due at the time and place of receipt; a credit sale isn't presumed, so the buyer must pay in full on acceptance (§ 2-607(1)).
Absent agreement, there's no credit period.
Practice with other suppliers isn't automatically a usage binding this seller; nothing shows a trade usage here.
Nothing in Article 2 conditions payment on resale.
topic: Wks 4–5 · Tender, delivery & payment — Time for payment

q: A seller delivers a used forklift; payment is due and demanded on delivery. The buyer takes the forklift but doesn't pay, promising to pay next week. Which statement is most accurate?
o: The buyer's right to keep the forklift depends on paying, so the seller may reclaim it.
Once the buyer takes possession, the seller's only remedy is to sue for the price.
The seller must wait a reasonable time before demanding payment.
The buyer may keep the forklift if it pays within ten days.
oe: Correct. Section 2-507(2): where payment is due and demanded on delivery, the buyer's right to retain or dispose of the goods is conditional on making the payment.
Section 2-507(2) lets the seller reclaim in a cash sale.
Payment was due and demanded on delivery.
Ten days relates to reclamation from an insolvent buyer (§ 2-702(2)), a different rule.
topic: Wks 4–5 · Tender, delivery & payment — Cash sale

q: A contract for 1,000 shirts lets the buyer specify the assortment of sizes and colors but doesn't say when. The seller asks for the assortment; the buyer stalls for weeks, past the time when the seller needed it to make the delivery date. What are the seller's rights?
o: Excused for the delay; may proceed reasonably or treat it as a breach.
The seller must wait for the buyer's specifications for as long as it takes.
The contract is void for indefiniteness because the assortment was never agreed.
The seller may ship any assortment it likes and the buyer must accept it.
oe: Correct. Section 2-311: assortment is at the buyer's option and must be specified in good faith and with commercial reasonableness. When needed cooperation isn't seasonably forthcoming, § 2-311(3) excuses the other party's delay and gives it these choices.
Section 2-311(3) protects the seller from a buyer's failure to cooperate.
Leaving particulars to one party is permitted under § 2-311(1).
The seller may proceed in a reasonable manner, not arbitrarily.
topic: Wks 4–5 · Tender, delivery & payment — Options and cooperation

q: A contract is “F.O.B. Chicago,” payment $10,000 by cashier's check, and silent on when payment is due. The seller ships under a negotiable bill of lading to its own order, and while the goods are still in transit, its agent demands payment against the bill. The buyer refuses to pay until the goods arrive and it can inspect them. Who is right?
o: The buyer: absent agreement, it may inspect on arrival before paying.
The seller: shipping under a negotiable bill of lading makes payment due against the documents.
The seller: in an F.O.B. shipment contract, payment is due when the goods are delivered to the carrier.
The buyer, but only because shipping under reservation is a breach of contract.
oe: Correct. Problem 4-8: § 2-310(a)–(b) and § 2-513(1). Shipping under reservation (§ 2-505) protects the seller's security interest, but nothing shows the buyer agreed to pay against documents, so it keeps the right to inspect before paying.
Merely using a bill of lading isn't an agreement to pay against documents.
Shipment contracts move risk at shipment, but payment is still due at receipt absent agreement.
Shipment under reservation is allowed (it's a breach only in a credit deal); the issue is the timing of payment.
topic: Wks 4–5 · Tender, delivery & payment — Shipment under reservation

q: A seller drives 100 bushels of wheat in its own truck to the buyer's facility and demands payment before the buyer may look at the wheat. The contract says nothing about inspection. The buyer refuses to pay until it inspects. Who is right?
o: The buyer: it may inspect before paying unless otherwise agreed.
The seller: payment on delivery means payment before inspection.
The seller, because the buyer can recover the price later if the wheat is defective.
Neither: the parties must split the cost of an independent inspection.
oe: Correct. Section 2-513(1) and § 2-503 cmt. 2. The seller's refusal impairs its tender (Problem 4-5(a)).
Payment on delivery doesn't eliminate the right to inspect; only terms like C.O.D. or payment against documents do.
That describes a contract requiring payment before inspection, which this isn't.
Inspection costs fall on the buyer, recoverable if the goods are rejected as nonconforming (§ 2-513(2)).
topic: Wks 4–5 · Inspection, acceptance & rejection — Payment before inspection

q: Same wheat. The buyer wants the wheat unloaded into its bins and a sample sent to a lab to test for genetic modification, which takes two weeks. The seller protests. The contract says nothing about GMOs. What's the best analysis?
o: Inspection must be reasonable; the buyer must reject in a reasonable time.
The buyer may test as long as it likes, because it hasn't accepted until it says so.
By unloading the wheat, the buyer has accepted it.
The seller must pay for the test, because the buyer has a right to inspect.
oe: Correct. Problem 4-5(b): taking possession isn't acceptance, but failing to reject after a reasonable opportunity to inspect is (§ 2-606(1)(b)). The buyer bears testing costs unless the goods are nonconforming and rejected (§ 2-513(2)).
Waiting too long to reject operates as acceptance.
Possession for inspection isn't acceptance.
Inspection costs are the buyer's unless the goods prove nonconforming and are rejected.
topic: Wks 4–5 · Inspection, acceptance & rejection — Reasonable manner of inspection

q: A contract requires payment C.O.D. On delivery, the buyer pays and then discovers on inspection that the goods are defective. Which statement is most accurate?
o: No inspection before paying, but paying isn't acceptance.
By paying, the buyer accepted the goods and can only sue for damages.
C.O.D. terms waive the buyer's right to inspect at any time.
The buyer could have refused to pay until it inspected, despite the C.O.D. term.
oe: Correct. Section 2-513(3)(a) removes inspection before payment for C.O.D. terms. Section 2-512(2): payment before inspection doesn't constitute acceptance or impair the buyer's right to inspect or its remedies.
Payment isn't acceptance (§ 2-512(2)).
They waive inspection before payment, not inspection itself.
C.O.D. eliminates inspection before payment.
topic: Wks 4–5 · Inspection, acceptance & rejection — C.O.D. and payment first

q: A contract requires the buyer to pay before inspecting. On delivery, the buyer can see without opening anything that the crates are smashed and leaking. Must the buyer pay first?
o: No: nonconformity excuses payment when it appears without inspection.
Yes: the contract requires payment before inspection, and the buyer can sue afterward.
Yes, unless the buyer proves the seller acted fraudulently.
No: a buyer is never required to pay before inspecting.
oe: Correct. Section 2-512(1) requires payment despite nonconformity unless (a) the nonconformity appears without inspection or (b) circumstances would justify an injunction against honor under § 5-109(b), essentially fraud.
The statute excuses payment when nonconformity appears without inspection.
Fraud is one exception; obvious nonconformity is another.
The parties may agree to payment before inspection; § 2-512 governs that agreement.
topic: Wks 4–5 · Inspection, acceptance & rejection — Payment before inspection excused

q: A restaurant receives a delivery of 30 cases of olive oil, stores them, and doesn't inspect or say anything for three months, though it could easily have opened a case. It then discovers the oil is rancid and tries to reject. Which statement is most accurate?
o: It accepted by failing to reject after a chance to inspect.
The restaurant may reject, because it never signified that the goods conformed.
The restaurant may reject, because possession alone never counts as acceptance.
The restaurant accepted when it took delivery.
oe: Correct. Section 2-606(1)(b): failing to reject after a reasonable opportunity to inspect is acceptance. The buyer may still have a damages claim, or possibly revocation under § 2-608, if it gives timely notice of breach.
Signifying acceptance is only one route; failure to reject is another.
Possession isn't acceptance, but failing to reject after a reasonable chance to inspect is.
Taking delivery for inspection isn't acceptance; the passage of time without rejection is.
topic: Wks 4–5 · Inspection, acceptance & rejection — What is acceptance

q: A buyer accepts a shipment of steel, then discovers that part of it doesn't meet the contract's tensile-strength spec. The defect doesn't substantially impair the shipment's value. What follows from the acceptance?
o: It must pay, but may recover damages if it gives timely notice.
The buyer may still reject the nonconforming portion, because the seller breached.
The buyer has waived all remedies by accepting.
The buyer may withhold the entire price until the seller cures.
oe: Correct. Under § 2-607, acceptance obligates payment (subsection 1), bars rejection (subsection 2), puts the burden of proving nonconformity on the buyer (subsection 4), and requires timely notice of breach or the buyer is barred from any remedy (subsection 3(a)). Damages run under § 2-714.
Acceptance precludes rejection.
Acceptance doesn't impair other remedies, provided the buyer gives notice.
The buyer must pay at the contract rate for accepted goods, subject to its damages claim.
topic: Wks 4–5 · Inspection, acceptance & rejection — Effects of acceptance

q: A buyer accepts a CNC machine after a brief test run. Two months later, a latent defect that couldn't reasonably have been found earlier causes the machine to fail every few hours, making it nearly useless for the buyer. The buyer promptly notifies the seller that it's revoking acceptance. Which statement is most accurate?
o: Likely proper: a substantial, hard-to-discover defect and prompt notice.
Revocation is impossible, because acceptance can never be undone.
Revocation is proper for any nonconformity, however minor.
Revocation requires the seller's consent.
oe: Correct. Section 2-608 allows revocation when nonconformity substantially impairs value, the goods were accepted on a reasonable assumption of cure or without discovery due to difficulty or seller's assurances, and revocation occurs within a reasonable time and before a substantial change not caused by defects. It's effective on notice.
Section 2-608 is precisely the window for undoing acceptance.
Revocation requires substantial impairment, unlike rejection.
Revocation is a buyer's right, effective on notice.
topic: Wks 4–5 · Inspection, acceptance & rejection — Revocation of acceptance

q: A buyer receives 500 laptops that don't conform. It decides to reject but doesn't tell the seller. Over the next two weeks, it lends 20 of the laptops to employees for daily use. Which statement is most accurate?
o: Ineffective without notice, and the use is an act of ownership.
The rejection is effective because the goods were nonconforming.
The buyer may use the goods until the seller picks them up.
The rejection is effective, but the buyer must pay rent for the laptops used.
oe: Correct. Section 2-602(1) requires rejection within a reasonable time and seasonable notice. After rejection, the buyer may not exercise ownership (§ 2-602(2)(a)) and must take reasonable care of goods in its possession (§ 2-602(2)(b)). Using them risks acceptance under § 2-606(1)(c).
Nonconformity gives a right to reject, but rejection still requires seasonable notice.
A rejecting buyer may not exercise ownership.
The bigger problems are missing notice and acts of ownership.
topic: Wks 4–5 · Inspection, acceptance & rejection — Effective rejection

q: A merchant buyer in Boston rightfully rejects a truckload of fresh strawberries from a California seller, which has no agent or place of business in Boston. The seller sends no instructions. The strawberries will spoil in two days. What must the buyer do?
o: Try to resell them for the seller's account.
Nothing: a rightfully rejecting buyer has no further obligations regarding the goods.
Hold them until the seller arrives, even if they spoil.
Keep them and pay a reduced price, since reselling them would be acceptance.
oe: Correct. Section 2-603 requires a merchant buyer, absent instructions, to make reasonable efforts to sell perishable goods for the seller's account (reimbursement plus usual commission, up to 10%). It's held only to good faith, and doing so isn't acceptance or conversion.
Merchant buyers have special duties with perishable goods when the seller has no local agent.
For perishables, the merchant buyer must try to resell.
Resale under § 2-603 isn't acceptance or conversion.
topic: Wks 4–5 · Inspection, acceptance & rejection — Merchant buyer's duties

q: On the 3rd, a buyer rejects a shipment, telling the seller only “not acceptable.” The contract delivery deadline is the 15th. Later, in litigation, the buyer relies on a mislabeling problem that a reasonable inspection would have revealed and the seller could easily have fixed. Can the buyer rely on that defect?
o: No: it failed to state a curable, discoverable defect.
Yes: a buyer may rely on any defect that actually existed.
Yes, because the seller should have asked what was wrong.
No, because any rejection must be in a signed writing listing every defect.
oe: Correct. Section 2-605(1)(a). Because there was time left to cure (§ 2-508(1)), a specific statement would have let the seller fix it. Between merchants, a seller's written request for a full statement of defects also triggers the bar (§ 2-605(1)(b)).
Section 2-605 bars unstated, curable, reasonably discoverable defects.
The statute puts the burden on the rejecting buyer to particularize.
No signed-writing requirement exists; the issue is particularizing curable defects.
topic: Wks 4–5 · Inspection, acceptance & rejection — Particularizing defects

q: A contract calls for delivery of 200 blue office chairs by June 30. On June 10, the seller delivers gray chairs, and the buyer rightfully rejects. On June 12, the seller tells the buyer it will deliver blue chairs by June 25. Must the buyer accept them?
o: Yes: the seller may cure within the contract time.
No: once the buyer rightfully rejects, the contract is over.
No: cure is available only if the seller had reasonable grounds to believe the gray chairs would be acceptable.
Yes, but the buyer may also recover damages for the gray chairs' nonconformity.
oe: Correct. Section 2-508(1). Cure softens the perfect tender rule, and it's why § 2-605 requires buyers to state curable defects.
The seller's right to cure survives rejection while time remains.
That's the § 2-508(2) test for cure after the contract time; within the time, § 2-508(1) applies.
A timely conforming cure generally leaves no breach to recover for.
topic: Wks 4–5 · Inspection, acceptance & rejection — Cure within the contract time

q: Variation: The seller delivers on June 30, the last day, a newer model of chair that it reasonably believed the buyer would accept because it's an upgrade at the same price. The buyer rejects. Can the seller still cure?
o: Yes, if the seller reasonably believed the tender acceptable.
No: cure is never available after the contract time expires.
No, because a different model is always a material breach.
Yes, and the buyer must accept the newer model as the cure.
oe: Correct. Section 2-508(2) extends cure beyond the contract time when the seller reasonably believed the nonconforming tender would be acceptable, with or without a money allowance.
Section 2-508(2) allows it in these circumstances.
Section 2-508(2) applies even to nonconforming tenders; the question is the seller's reasonable belief.
The seller gets time to substitute a conforming tender, not to force the newer model on the buyer.
topic: Wks 4–5 · Inspection, acceptance & rejection — Cure after the deadline
pre: A contract calls for delivery of 200 blue office chairs by June 30. On June 10, the seller delivers gray chairs, and the buyer rightfully rejects. On June 12, the seller tells the buyer it will deliver blue chairs by June 25. Must the buyer accept them?

q: A buyer orders 50 dining sets (each a table and six chairs) for its hotel. One table arrives cracked; everything else conforms. Which options does the buyer have?
o: Reject the whole, accept the whole, or accept any commercial units and reject the rest.
Only accept the shipment and sue for damages, because the defect is minor.
Only reject the cracked table, keeping the chairs that came with it.
Reject the whole shipment only if the defect substantially impairs its value.
oe: Correct. Under § 2-601's perfect tender rule, if goods fail in any respect, the buyer may reject the whole, accept the whole, or accept some commercial units and reject the rest. A dining set may be one commercial unit, so accepting part of one is accepting the whole unit.
Article 2 uses perfect tender, not substantial performance, for single-delivery contracts.
If the set is a commercial unit, accepting part of it accepts the whole unit.
Substantial impairment is the installment-contract test, not the rule here.
topic: Wks 4–5 · Inspection, acceptance & rejection — Perfect tender and commercial units

q: A buyer receives a conforming shipment of 300 helmets but, because the market price has dropped, promptly notifies the seller that it rejects them and holds them for pickup. Which statement is most accurate?
o: Effective but wrongful: the buyer has breached.
The rejection is ineffective, so the buyer has accepted the helmets.
The rejection is rightful, because a buyer may reject for any reason within a reasonable time.
The rejection is void, and the buyer must pay for the helmets as if accepted.
oe: Correct. An effective rejection (timely, with notice) can still be wrongful if the goods conform. That's the buyer's breach (§ 2-301; § 2-703). Rightful rejection of nonconforming goods preserves the buyer's remedies (§ 2-711).
An effective rejection isn't acceptance, even if wrongful.
Rejection is rightful only for nonconforming goods.
The seller's remedies for wrongful rejection are damages under § 2-703 and related sections, not automatically the price.
topic: Wks 4–5 · Inspection, acceptance & rejection — Wrongful but effective rejection

q: A contract calls for 12 monthly deliveries of 1,000 brake pads. The third installment includes 40 pads with a minor surface flaw that the seller can easily replace within days, and the seller offers to do so. The buyer wants to reject the installment and cancel the contract. Which statement is most accurate?
o: Neither: the defect is minor, curable, and doesn't impair the whole contract.
The buyer may reject the installment, because any nonconformity allows rejection.
The buyer may cancel the whole contract, because any breach of an installment is a breach of the whole.
The buyer must accept all future installments but may refuse to pay for this one.
oe: Correct. Section 2-612 replaces perfect tender for installment contracts with substantial impairment, and cure matters.
That's perfect tender, which doesn't govern installment contracts.
Only a nonconformity substantially impairing the whole contract allows cancellation.
Withholding payment for an accepted installment isn't allowed; the buyer's remedy is damages.
topic: Wks 4–5 · Inspection, acceptance & rejection — Installment contracts

q: A farm-supply merchant sells 100 bushels of wheat and calls the buyer to say the wheat is ready for pickup at the merchant's facility. Before the buyer arrives, a fire destroys the facility and the wheat. Neither party breached, and nothing was agreed about risk. Who bears the loss?
o: The seller: a merchant seller keeps the risk until the buyer actually receives the goods.
The buyer: risk passed when the seller tendered by holding the goods and notifying the buyer.
The buyer, because title passed when the contract was made.
They split it equally, because neither was at fault.
oe: Correct. Under § 2-509(3), with a merchant seller, risk passes on the buyer's receipt (physical possession). Comment 3: the merchant still controls the goods and is likely insured, while the buyer isn't (Problem 4-6(b)).
That's the rule for non-merchant sellers.
Risk of loss doesn't follow title.
Article 2 assigns the risk to one party; it doesn't split it.
topic: Wks 4–5 · Risk of loss — Merchant seller, no receipt

q: Variation: The seller is a retired farmer, not a merchant, selling wheat left over from his last harvest. He properly tendered by holding the wheat at his barn and notifying the buyer. Fire then destroys the barn before pickup. Who bears the loss?
o: The buyer: with a non-merchant seller, risk passes on tender of delivery, so the buyer must pay.
The seller: risk stays with any seller until the buyer receives the goods.
Neither: § 2-613 avoids the contract because the goods were destroyed without fault.
The seller, because the barn was within the seller's control.
oe: Correct. Section 2-509(3): non-merchant → risk passes on tender. Here tender was complete, so the buyer bears the loss and owes the price (§ 2-709(1)(a)). Merchant status is outcome-determinative on these facts.
That's the merchant-seller rule.
Section 2-613 applies only if the casualty occurs before risk passes. Here it had passed.
Control is a policy reason behind the merchant rule, but the statute applies tender for non-merchants.
topic: Wks 4–5 · Risk of loss — Non-merchant seller
pre: A farm-supply merchant sells 100 bushels of wheat and calls the buyer to say the wheat is ready for pickup at the merchant's facility. Before the buyer arrives, a fire destroys the facility and the wheat. Neither party breached, and nothing was agreed about risk. Who bears the loss?

q: A seller loads 100 bushels of fungible wheat onto its own truck to deliver to the buyer's facility. On the way, the truck catches fire and the wheat is destroyed. Who bears the loss, and must the seller deliver other wheat?
o: The seller bears the loss, and because the wheat is fungible, it must still tender substitute wheat or be in breach.
The buyer bears the loss, because the goods were delivered to a carrier.
The seller bears the loss, but the contract is avoided because the goods were destroyed without fault.
The buyer bears the loss, because tender began when the seller loaded the truck.
oe: Correct. The seller's own truck isn't a carrier, so § 2-509(3) applies. Whether merchant (no receipt) or non-merchant (tender not complete until the goods are at the buyer's disposition at the place of delivery), the seller bears the risk. Fungible goods mean § 2-613 gives no excuse (Problem 4-6(a)).
A seller transporting its own goods isn't a carrier.
Section 2-613 requires goods identified when the contract was made; fungible wheat isn't.
Risk passes at the completion of tender, not its start.
topic: Wks 4–5 · Risk of loss — Seller's own truck

q: A buyer pays a merchant seller the full price for a riding mower when the contract is signed. The seller tells the buyer the mower is ready, and the buyer says it will pick it up next week. Before pickup, a storm destroys the mower at the seller's lot. The seller argues risk passed because the buyer had paid and been notified. Is the seller right?
o: No: a merchant seller keeps the risk until receipt.
Yes: once the buyer pays in full, risk passes to it.
Yes: notice that the goods are ready completes tender, which shifts risk.
No, but only because a storm is an act of God that excuses both parties.
oe: Correct. Section 2-509(3) cmt. 3 says a merchant seller retains risk until actual receipt even if the buyer has paid in full and been notified the goods are at its disposal (Capshaw v. Hickman).
Payment doesn't shift risk under § 2-509(3).
Tender shifts risk only for non-merchant sellers.
The answer turns on the merchant rule, not on the nature of the casualty.
topic: Wks 4–5 · Risk of loss — Prepayment

q: Under a shipment contract, a seller ships nonconforming goods (the wrong grade of lumber) by carrier. A flood destroys the shipment in transit. The buyer hadn't yet seen the goods. Who bears the loss?
o: The seller, because the nonconforming tender keeps risk on it.
The buyer: risk passed when the goods were delivered to the carrier under a shipment contract.
The carrier, because the goods were in its possession.
The buyer, unless it had already rejected the goods before the flood.
oe: Correct. Section 2-510(1) overrides § 2-509's shipment-contract rule when the seller breaches with a nonconforming tender.
That's the no-breach rule; the seller's breach changes the result.
The carrier may be liable under other law, but between buyer and seller, § 2-510(1) puts the risk on the seller.
No rejection is needed; the right to reject is enough to keep risk on the seller.
topic: Wks 4–5 · Risk of loss — Nonconforming tender

q: A seller has identified 500 conforming bicycles to a contract. Before risk would normally pass, the buyer repudiates. Two weeks later, while the seller is arranging resale, a warehouse fire destroys the bicycles. The seller's insurance covers 70% of their value. Who bears the uninsured 30%?
o: The buyer, for a commercially reasonable time.
The seller, because risk hadn't yet passed under § 2-509.
The buyer, for the full value regardless of insurance.
The seller's insurer and the buyer split it equally.
oe: Correct. Section 2-510(3): if the buyer repudiates or breaches as to conforming goods already identified to the contract, the seller may treat the risk as resting on the buyer for a commercially reasonable time, to the extent of any deficiency in the seller's effective insurance.
Section 2-510(3) shifts risk to the breaching buyer for a time.
The shift extends only to the deficiency in the seller's insurance.
The statute shifts only the uninsured portion to the buyer.
topic: Wks 4–5 · Risk of loss — Buyer's breach

q: A buyer accepts a delivered boat, discovers a latent hull defect that substantially impairs its value, and rightfully revokes acceptance. While the seller arranges to pick it up, a storm destroys the boat at the buyer's dock. The buyer's insurance covers half its value. Who bears the rest?
o: The seller, to the extent the buyer's insurance falls short.
The buyer, because it had possession when the storm hit.
The seller, for the full value including the insured half.
The buyer, because revocation is effective only after the seller retakes the goods.
oe: Correct. Section 2-510(2). Risk-of-loss rules ask who is likely to have insurance, and both parties can have an insurable interest at once (§ 2-501).
Possession isn't decisive once the buyer rightfully revokes.
The shift extends only to the buyer's insurance deficiency.
Revocation is effective on notice, and § 2-510(2) then applies.
topic: Wks 4–5 · Risk of loss — Revocation and risk

q: A South Dakota manufacturer contracts to make custom windows for a building in New York. The contract says the windows will be “shipped properly crated for cross-country motor freight and delivered to the construction site in New York.” The seller properly packages them, delivers them to a carrier with a proper contract, and notifies the buyer. They're destroyed in transit. Who bears the loss?
o: The buyer: “delivered to” only names the destination of a shipment contract.
The seller: naming the delivery location makes it a destination contract.
The seller, because custom goods are always the seller's risk until installed.
The carrier, because the buyer and seller agreed the carrier would bear the risk.
oe: Correct. Windows, Inc. v. Jordan Panel Systems (Problem 4-7(a)). Shipment contracts are presumed (§ 2-503 cmt. 5); risk passed on due delivery to the carrier (§ 2-509(1)(a)). The buyer's recourse is against the carrier.
Every shipping contract names a destination; that alone doesn't create a destination contract.
No such rule; the shipment presumption governs.
The contract says nothing about the carrier bearing risk; between the parties, the buyer bears it.
topic: Wks 4–5 · Risk of loss — Shipment presumption

q: Variation: The contract instead says the windows will be “delivered at the construction site in New York.” What's the best argument, and the likely approach?
o: Arguably a destination contract, but the shipment presumption remains strong.
“Delivered at” always creates a destination contract.
The wording doesn't matter; only F.O.B. terms create destination contracts.
“Delivered at” makes the carrier the buyer's agent, shifting risk to the buyer.
oe: Correct. Problem 4-7(b) shows how a slight wording change matters. To draft a clear destination contract, use “F.O.B. Buyer's construction site” or say the seller bears risk until tender there.
Courts read the language contextually; the shipment presumption remains.
Other language can create a destination contract if it clearly allocates transit risk to the seller.
The carrier's status isn't the issue; the question is whether the seller agreed to tender at the destination.
topic: Wks 4–5 · Risk of loss — “Delivered at”
pre: A South Dakota manufacturer contracts to make custom windows for a building in New York. The contract says the windows will be “shipped properly crated for cross-country motor freight and delivered to the construction site in New York.” The seller properly packages them, delivers them to a carrier with a proper contract, and notifies the buyer. They're destroyed in transit. Who bears the loss?

q: Under a shipment contract, a seller ships windows in flimsy, inadequate crates, and they're destroyed in transit because of the bad packaging. Who bears the loss?
o: The seller, because its bad packaging caused the loss.
The buyer: in a shipment contract, all transit losses fall on the buyer.
The carrier, because it accepted the goods for transport.
The buyer, because packaging failures never justify rejection.
oe: Correct. Section 2-504(a) and its last sentence; the nonconformity triggers § 2-510(1) (Problem 4-7(d)(1)).
Not when the seller's breach of its shipment duties causes the loss.
Between buyer and seller, the seller's packaging breach keeps risk on the seller.
They do when material delay or loss ensues.
topic: Wks 4–5 · Risk of loss — Improper packaging

q: Variation: The windows were improperly packaged, but they were destroyed when the carrier's truck crashed through the carrier's negligence; the packaging didn't contribute to the loss. Who bears the loss?
o: The buyer, because the packaging didn't cause the loss.
The seller: any breach of § 2-504 keeps the risk on the seller.
The seller, because improper packaging is always a nonconforming tender.
The carrier, and neither party bears any loss.
oe: Correct. Windows v. Jordan Panel: because the packaging didn't cause the loss, there was no right of rejection, so § 2-510(1) didn't apply and risk had passed to the buyer.
Only if material delay or loss ensues from the breach.
The court asked whether the packaging caused the loss.
Between buyer and seller, the buyer bears it; it can pursue the carrier.
topic: Wks 4–5 · Risk of loss — Bad packaging, carrier's fault
pre: Under a shipment contract, a seller ships windows in flimsy, inadequate crates, and they're destroyed in transit because of the bad packaging. Who bears the loss?

q: Which shipping term creates a destination contract, so that the seller bears the risk of loss during transit?
o: “F.O.B. Buyer's warehouse, Denver,” the buyer's city.
“F.O.B. Seller's plant, Ohio.”
“C.I.F. Port of Baltimore,” with the seller paying for insurance and freight.
“Seller to pay all freight charges to Buyer's plant.”
oe: Correct. F.O.B. the buyer's location is a destination contract: the seller must transport the goods there at its expense and risk and tender delivery (§ 2-319(1)(b)). F.O.B. the seller's location, C.I.F., and C. & F. are shipment contracts.
F.O.B. the place of shipment is a shipment contract (§ 2-319(1)(a)).
C.I.F. is a shipment contract even though the seller pays freight and insurance.
A term requiring the seller to pay freight doesn't by itself make a destination contract.
topic: Wks 4–5 · Risk of loss — F.O.B. and C.I.F.

q: A contract is “C.I.F. Port of Seattle.” The seller loads conforming goods, obtains a negotiable bill of lading and insurance payable to the buyer, and tenders the documents while the ship is at sea. The buyer refuses to pay until the goods arrive and it can inspect them. Who is right?
o: The seller: C.I.F. requires payment against documents.
The buyer: a buyer may always inspect before paying.
The buyer, because the seller bears the risk until the goods arrive under C.I.F.
The seller, but only if the buyer also accepts the goods on arrival.
oe: Correct. Section 2-320(4) and § 2-513(3). Paying against documents waives inspection before payment, not inspection before acceptance (§ 2-512(2)). By contrast, an “ex-ship” term doesn't pass risk until the goods leave the ship's tackle (§ 2-322).
C.I.F. terms eliminate inspection before payment.
C.I.F. is a shipment contract; risk passed at shipment.
Paying against documents doesn't count as acceptance; the buyer may still inspect and reject.
topic: Wks 4–5 · Risk of loss — C.I.F. payment and ex-ship

q: A contract is “F.A.S. vessel, Port of Houston.” The buyer never tells the seller which vessel or berth to use, and the sailing date passes. What is the buyer's failure?
o: A failure of cooperation under § 2-311.
Nothing, because under F.A.S. the seller must choose the vessel.
An anticipatory repudiation, as a matter of law.
A breach of the warranty of merchantability.
oe: Correct. Under § 2-319(2)–(3), F.A.S. requires the seller to deliver alongside the vessel, and the buyer must seasonably give needed instructions (berth, vessel name, sailing date). Failing to do so is a failure of cooperation.
The buyer must name the vessel and give instructions.
It's a failure of cooperation; whether it rises to repudiation depends on more.
This has nothing to do with the goods' quality.
topic: Wks 4–5 · Risk of loss — F.A.S. and buyer's instructions

q: A buyer's order says “Ship to Buyer, Council Bluffs,” with a routing and freight rate. The seller's later invoice says “F.O.B. delivered $1.20 rate.” The seller loads a carrier-supplied rail car, the carrier's agent signs a bill of lading, and a fire destroys the car before the carrier moves it. The buyer argues it was a destination contract. Who likely bears the loss?
o: The buyer: the order formed a shipment contract.
The seller: the invoice's “F.O.B. delivered” term made it a destination contract.
The seller, because the goods hadn't begun moving.
The carrier, which signed the bill of lading.
oe: Correct. Problem 4-9: risk passed under § 2-509(1)(a) when the goods were duly delivered to the carrier (loaded into its car with a signed bill of lading).
The invoice came after formation and would be at most a § 2-207 proposal; in context it addressed freight charges.
Due delivery to the carrier, not movement, passes risk in a shipment contract.
Between the parties, risk had passed to the buyer.
topic: Wks 4–5 · Risk of loss — Formation and shipping terms

q: An owner sells a horse that is in transit with a carrier and hands the buyer a non-negotiable bill of lading naming the owner as consignee. Two hours later, the horse is killed in an accident. Who bears the loss?
o: Likely the owner, because a reasonable time to present hadn't passed.
The buyer: risk passed when it received the bill of lading.
The buyer, because the horse was in a carrier's possession under a shipment contract.
The carrier, which issued the bill of lading.
oe: Correct. Sections 2-509(2)(c) and 2-503(4)(b) (Problem 4-11). Risk passes immediately on receipt of a negotiable document or on the bailee's acknowledgment of the buyer's right to possession.
That's the rule for negotiable documents.
The goods were to be delivered without being moved by the seller's shipment; the bailee rules apply.
Between buyer and seller, the risk stays with the owner for now.
topic: Wks 4–5 · Risk of loss — Goods held by a bailee

q: Variation: An appliance seller with 200 ovens in a warehouse offers to indorse and deliver to the buyer a negotiable warehouse receipt covering all of them. The buyer says it wants to pay for each oven as it resells them. Who is right?
o: The seller: tendering the receipt is proper, with payment due on tender.
The buyer: buyers may pay for goods held by a bailee as they take them.
The seller, but only if the warehouse moves the ovens to the buyer's store.
The buyer, because a warehouse receipt isn't the goods themselves.
oe: Correct. Problem 4-10: § 2-503(4)(a), § 2-310, and § 2-307. Risk would pass on the buyer's receipt of the negotiable document (§ 2-509(2)(a)).
Absent agreement, delivery is in a single lot and payment is due on tender.
Tender of a negotiable document is tender of goods held by a bailee without moving them.
A negotiable document controls the goods; tendering it is proper tender.
topic: Wks 4–5 · Risk of loss — Negotiable warehouse receipt
pre: An owner sells a horse that is in transit with a carrier and hands the buyer a non-negotiable bill of lading naming the owner as consignee. Two hours later, the horse is killed in an accident. Who bears the loss?

q: A seller's goods are destroyed before the buyer gets them, and you must decide who bears the loss. The contract says: “Risk of loss passes to Buyer when Seller notifies Buyer the goods are ready.” The seller gave that notice, and its tender conformed. What should you do first?
o: Apply the parties' agreement: the risk rules of § 2-509 are subject to contrary agreement, so risk passed on the notice.
Apply § 2-509(3): a merchant seller keeps the risk until the buyer receives the goods.
Ask who held title when the goods were destroyed.
Apply § 2-510, because the destruction of the goods is a breach.
oe: Correct. The analysis runs: identify the seller's tender obligation; ask whether anyone breached (§ 2-510 vs. § 2-509); then apply the right § 2-509 rule (carrier, bailee, or direct tender). But § 2-509(4) makes all of this subject to the parties' contrary agreement, which can include trade usage or course of dealing.
That default yields to the parties' express agreement on risk.
Risk of loss doesn't turn on title.
A casualty isn't a breach; § 2-510 applies only if a party has breached.
topic: Wks 4–5 · Risk of loss — Order of analysis

q: Before risk of loss passes, the specific antique clock a dealer agreed to sell (identified when the contract was made) is destroyed by lightning. A month earlier, under a different contract, a dealer's buyer had already received a different clock before a fire destroyed it at the buyer's home. What are the parties' obligations?
o: The first contract is avoided; the second buyer must pay.
Both dealers must deliver substitute clocks.
Both buyers are excused from paying.
The first dealer must pay damages, because it bore the risk of loss.
oe: Correct. Section 2-613 avoids the contract for unique, identified goods destroyed without fault while the seller bears the risk. Once risk passes, the buyer must pay the price (§ 2-709(1)(a)).
Substitutes are required for fungible goods, not unique identified goods; and the second loss was the buyer's.
The second buyer bore the risk when the fire occurred.
Bearing the risk means losing the clock's value; § 2-613 excuses the dealer from damages for non-delivery.
topic: Wks 4–5 · Risk of loss — Who must still perform

q: A buyer contracts to buy a specific used crane sitting in the seller's yard. The contract is signed, but the seller keeps title and possession until payment next month. Can both parties insure the crane?
o: Yes: both have an insurable interest in the crane.
No: only the party with title has an insurable interest.
Only the buyer, because the goods have been identified to its contract.
Only the seller, until risk of loss passes to the buyer.
oe: Correct. Section 2-501. Because both may insure at once, the risk-of-loss rules consider who is likely to have insurance, and § 2-510 shifts risk only to the extent of insurance deficiencies.
The buyer gets a special property and insurable interest on identification.
The seller retains an insurable interest while it holds title or a security interest.
Insurable interest arises on identification, independent of risk of loss.
topic: Wks 4–5 · Risk of loss — Insurable interest

q: A homeowner takes a $3,000 rug home “on approval” for a week to see how it looks; a boutique takes 20 rugs from a wholesaler for resale, with the right to return unsold ones. Both sets of rugs are damaged by fire before any decision. Who bears the loss in each case?
o: The seller bears the first loss; the boutique bears the second.
The seller bears both losses, because the buyers hadn't committed to keep the rugs.
The buyer bears both losses, because both had possession.
The homeowner bears the loss, because trial use counts as acceptance.
oe: Correct. Goods delivered primarily for use are on approval; for resale, sale or return (§ 2-326). On approval, title and risk stay with the seller until acceptance (§ 2-327(1)). In sale or return, the buyer bears the risk, and return is at its risk and expense (§ 2-327(2)).
In a sale or return, the buyer has the goods at its risk.
On approval, risk stays with the seller until acceptance.
Trial use isn't acceptance under § 2-327(1)(a).
topic: Wks 4–5 · Risk of loss — Sale on approval vs. sale or return

q: A supply contract states: (1) “Seller may cure defects within 45 days of notice,” replacing the UCC's reasonable-time standard; and (2) “Seller shall have no obligation to act reasonably in performing this contract.” Which provisions are enforceable?
o: Only the first: duties of reasonableness can't be disclaimed.
Both: parties may vary any UCC provision by agreement.
Neither: the UCC's reasonable-time and reasonableness standards are mandatory.
Only the second, because provisions without “unless otherwise agreed” can't be varied.
oe: Correct. Section 1-302(a) lets parties vary the Code's effect, but § 1-302(b) bars disclaiming good faith, diligence, reasonableness, and care, while allowing standards for measuring them and specific times that aren't manifestly unreasonable.
Section 1-302(b) carves out good faith, diligence, reasonableness, and care.
Specific times can replace reasonable-time standards if not manifestly unreasonable.
Section 1-302(c) says the absence of that phrase doesn't imply a provision can't be varied.
topic: Wks 5–7 · Variation by agreement & disclaimers — Variation by agreement

q: A seller and buyer sign a contract stating: (1) “The parties agree this transaction is a sale governed by Article 2,” for what is in substance a secured loan; (2) “No court may refuse to enforce any term on grounds of unconscionability”; (3) “Any good-faith purchaser from Buyer takes subject to Seller's rights”; and (4) “Seller's warranty claims must be brought within 18 months.” Which clause is most likely enforceable?
o: Clause 4, because it shortens the limitations period to over a year.
Clause 1, because parties are free to choose which law governs their deal.
Clause 2, because sophisticated parties may waive unconscionability defenses.
Clause 3, because it allocates risk between the parties.
oe: Correct. Section 2-725(1) permits that. Per Problem 5-1(b), parties can't vary scope (§ 2-102, so a disguised security interest stays in Article 9), unconscionability (§ 2-302), or third parties' rights (§ 2-403). The formation rules and § 2-201 also can't be varied.
Parties can't make Article 2 apply by labeling a security interest a sale.
The court's power under § 2-302 can't be contracted away.
Buyer and seller can't alter third parties' rights under § 2-403 by their own contract.
topic: Wks 5–7 · Variation by agreement & disclaimers — Non-variable rules

q: A trucking company will buy all the diesel it needs for 12 months from a fuel supplier, at a price the supplier sets at each delivery. You represent the trucking company. Which clause best protects it while remaining enforceable?
o: A price capped at an objective market benchmark or its best customer price.
“Seller shall have no duty of good faith in setting the price.”
“The price shall be whatever Buyer considers fair.”
“Seller shall set the price in good faith.”
oe: Correct. Problem 5-1(a)(1): § 2-305(2) requires a seller-set price to be fixed in good faith; § 1-302(b) lets the parties define that standard if not manifestly unreasonable. Tying it to objective, verifiable benchmarks does so.
Good faith can't be disclaimed.
That shifts unfettered discretion to the buyer and is likely manifestly unreasonable and indefinite.
That only restates the default; it adds no protection.
topic: Wks 5–7 · Variation by agreement & disclaimers — Defining good faith in drafting

q: Variation: Now you represent the fuel supplier in the same requirements deal. Which clause best protects it?
o: A stated estimate with minimums, maximums, and a definition of requirements.
“Buyer's requirements shall be whatever Seller decides to supply.”
“Buyer waives the good-faith limit on its requirements.”
No clause; § 2-306's disproportion test already gives the seller complete protection.
oe: Correct. Problem 5-1(a)(2): this tracks § 2-306's own concepts (an estimate as the center of variation and minimums and maximums as clear limits, cmt. 3), so it isn't manifestly unreasonable.
That makes the buyer's commitment illusory and is likely manifestly unreasonable.
That hurts the seller, and good faith can't be disclaimed anyway.
The default test is vague; an estimate with limits is far more predictable.
topic: Wks 5–7 · Variation by agreement & disclaimers — Protecting the requirements seller
pre: A trucking company will buy all the diesel it needs for 12 months from a fuel supplier, at a price the supplier sets at each delivery. You represent the trucking company. Which clause best protects it while remaining enforceable?

q: A seller sends a buyer a sample of fabric. The buyer inspects it and signs the seller's form, which states: “Seller makes no express warranties.” The delivered fabric doesn't match the sample. Is the seller liable?
o: Likely yes: an irreconcilable disclaimer of a sample warranty is inoperative.
No: a signed disclaimer of express warranties always controls.
No: sample warranties can be disclaimed only by conspicuous language, and this was signed.
Yes, but only because the seller is a merchant.
oe: Correct. Section 2-316(1). It's “almost oxymoronic” to disclaim an express warranty; the seller avoids one by not making it. The seller's real defense, if any, is the parol evidence rule.
A disclaimer that can't be reconciled with an express warranty is inoperative.
Conspicuousness isn't the test for express warranties; reconciliation is.
Express warranties don't depend on merchant status.
topic: Wks 5–7 · Variation by agreement & disclaimers — Disclaiming express warranties

q: A dealer's signed contract states, in large bold capitals just above the signature line: “THERE ARE NO WARRANTIES WHICH EXTEND BEYOND THE DESCRIPTION ON THE FACE HEREOF.” Which implied warranties have been effectively disclaimed?
o: Fitness only, because merchantability wasn't mentioned.
Both merchantability and fitness, because the clause is conspicuous.
Neither, because disclaimers must use the words “as is.”
Merchantability only, because fitness can never be disclaimed.
oe: Correct. The quoted language is the statute's example for excluding fitness, which needs only a conspicuous writing. Merchantability under subsection (2) must be mentioned by name; if written, conspicuously.
Conspicuousness is necessary but not sufficient for merchantability; the word must appear.
“As is” is one method; the statutory language works for fitness.
Fitness can be disclaimed by a conspicuous writing.
topic: Wks 5–7 · Variation by agreement & disclaimers — Disclaiming merchantability

q: Before a sale, a hardware dealer tells a buyer face-to-face: “I'm not giving you any warranty of merchantability on this generator.” Nothing is in writing. Is merchantability disclaimed?
o: Yes: oral disclaimers that mention merchantability work.
No: all warranty disclaimers must be in writing.
No: an oral disclaimer can never be conspicuous.
Yes, and it also disclaims fitness for a particular purpose.
oe: Correct. Section 2-316(2). By contrast, a fitness disclaimer must be in a conspicuous writing.
Merchantability disclaimers may be oral.
Conspicuousness applies only to written disclaimers.
Fitness disclaimers must be in a conspicuous writing.
topic: Wks 5–7 · Variation by agreement & disclaimers — Oral disclaimer

q: A contract states, in bold just above the signatures: “There are no warranties, express or implied, included as a part of this transaction.” The seller is a merchant. Does this disclaim merchantability?
o: Not under (2); under (3)(a), courts split.
Yes: any conspicuous statement that there are no implied warranties disclaims merchantability.
No, and it can't disclaim fitness either, because fitness must be named.
Yes, because the words “express or implied” cover all warranties.
oe: Correct. Problem 5-2(C)(1). The same language works for fitness, which needs only a conspicuous writing.
Under (2), merchantability must be mentioned; the (3)(a) route is contested.
Fitness disclaimers need no magic words.
Courts disagree whether general language satisfies (3)(a).
topic: Wks 5–7 · Variation by agreement & disclaimers — General “no warranties” language

q: A used-TV seller's form states, in the same font as everything else: “The goods are sold as is.” Some of the TVs came from a flood, and the seller couldn't rule out water damage. A buyer claims the implied warranty of merchantability. What is the most likely result?
o: Likely disclaimed: “as is” excludes implied warranties.
The disclaimer fails, because it doesn't mention merchantability.
The disclaimer fails, because “as is” language must be in a separately signed writing.
The disclaimer works and also disclaims the warranty of title.
oe: Correct. Problem 5-2(C)(2). The circumstances (flood-sourced goods) support it. But “unless the circumstances indicate otherwise” lets fraud defeat “as is” (Sorchaga v. Ride Auto).
“As is” is an alternative to the (2) route and needs no magic words.
No such requirement exists.
“As is” doesn't disclaim title (§ 2-312(2)).
topic: Wks 5–7 · Variation by agreement & disclaimers — “As is”

q: A used-equipment dealer tells a buyer, “Look over this compressor as thoroughly as you want before you buy.” The buyer, a layperson, glances at it but doesn't run it. A hidden internal crack, which only testing would reveal, later causes failure. Is the implied warranty excluded by examination?
o: No: latent defects requiring testing aren't excluded.
Yes: because the buyer had the chance to inspect, all implied warranties are excluded.
Yes: any examination by the buyer, however brief, excludes all implied warranties.
No, because examination can only exclude the warranty of fitness.
oe: Correct. Section 2-316(3)(b). A professional buyer is charged with what a professional should notice; latent defects needing testing aren't excluded. Mere availability for inspection isn't enough; the seller must demand examination (cmt. 8).
Only defects an examination ought to have revealed are excluded.
The exclusion is limited to defects the examination should have revealed.
It can exclude implied warranties generally, but only as to discoverable defects.
topic: Wks 5–7 · Variation by agreement & disclaimers — Examination

q: A seller says to a buyer, “Feel free to look at the truck if you like,” and the buyer declines. Another seller says, “I insist that you inspect this truck thoroughly before signing,” and that buyer refuses. Which seller can rely on § 2-316(3)(b)?
o: Only the second, because the seller demanded inspection.
Both, because each buyer declined the chance to inspect.
Neither, because refusal to examine never excludes warranties.
Only the first, because the buyer voluntarily chose not to look.
oe: Correct. Comment 8 to § 2-316. Course of dealing, course of performance, or trade usage can also exclude implied warranties (§ 2-316(3)(c)).
An invitation isn't a demand.
A refusal after the seller's demand does, as to defects examination would have revealed.
The statute requires the seller's demand.
topic: Wks 5–7 · Variation by agreement & disclaimers — Refusal to examine

q: A seller's one-page form has a disclaimer of merchantability on the back, in capital letters larger than the surrounding text, under the heading “TERMS AND CONDITIONS.” The front says only, “Subject to terms and conditions stated herein.” Who decides whether the disclaimer is conspicuous, and how?
o: The court, asking whether a reasonable person ought to have noticed it.
The jury decides, based on whether the buyer actually read it.
It's automatically conspicuous because it's in capital letters larger than the surrounding text.
It's automatically inconspicuous because it's on the back of the form.
oe: Correct. Section 1-201(b)(10) makes conspicuousness a question for the court. Larger capitals help, but placement on the back with only a vague reference on the front may undercut it (Problem 5-4).
It's for the court, and the test is what a reasonable person ought to have noticed.
Type is one example of conspicuousness, but the totality of circumstances governs.
Placement is a factor, not a rule.
topic: Wks 5–7 · Variation by agreement & disclaimers — Conspicuousness

q: An experienced commercial fisherman tells a dealer his boat's size and weight; on the dealer's recommendation, he buys a diesel engine. At delivery, he signs the dealer's standard receipt, which says on the back in large capitals: “SELLER DISCLAIMS ALL IMPLIED WARRANTIES, INCLUDING MERCHANTABILITY.” The engine smokes constantly and is underpowered for the boat. What is the fisherman's best argument?
o: The disclaimer came after formation and never became part of the deal.
The disclaimer is void because it doesn't mention fitness for a particular purpose.
The disclaimer is void because it's in capitals, which makes it misleading.
Implied warranties can't be disclaimed for commercial goods.
oe: Correct. Problem 5-4(A). Threshold questions come first: did the warranties arise (merchantability, yes; fitness, yes, given the disclosed purpose and reliance), and is the disclaimer part of the contract (§§ 2-207, 2-209)? Only then is § 2-316 compliance relevant.
“All implied warranties” covers fitness, and no magic words are needed for it.
Capitals support conspicuousness; they don't invalidate a disclaimer.
They can be, if properly done and part of the contract.
topic: Wks 5–7 · Variation by agreement & disclaimers — Disclaimer on a delivery receipt

q: Variation: The seller isn't a merchant in engines at all; it's a boatyard selling one engine it happened to have. Which warranties could the fisherman claim?
o: Only fitness, because merchantability requires a merchant seller.
Both, because the boatyard sold the engine in the course of business.
Neither, because only merchants make implied warranties.
Only merchantability, because fitness requires an expert seller.
oe: Correct. Problem 5-4(C): without a merchant seller, no merchantability warranty arises, so the disclaimer is irrelevant to it; fitness can still arise.
Merchantability requires merchant status as to goods of that kind.
Fitness doesn't require a merchant.
Fitness requires reason to know of the purpose and reliance, not merchant status.
topic: Wks 5–7 · Variation by agreement & disclaimers — Non-merchant dealer
pre: An experienced commercial fisherman tells a dealer his boat's size and weight; on the dealer's recommendation, he buys a diesel engine. At delivery, he signs the dealer's standard receipt, which says on the back in large capitals: “SELLER DISCLAIMS ALL IMPLIED WARRANTIES, INCLUDING MERCHANTABILITY.” The engine smokes constantly and is underpowered for the boat. What is the fisherman's best argument?

q: Variation: The buyer is a consumer buying the engine for a pleasure boat, and the dealer also gave a written limited warranty. Which point most strengthens the consumer's position on the disclaimer?
o: The term was only a proposal, and Magnuson-Moss bars the disclaimer.
Consumers can't be bound by any written disclaimer under the UCC.
The disclaimer is valid, because consumers are held to what they sign.
The consumer can avoid the disclaimer only by proving fraud.
oe: Correct. Problem 5-4(B). Section 2-207(2)'s merchant rule doesn't apply; consumer-protection law and stronger unconscionability arguments also help. The continuum puts prepackaged consumer goods at the most-protected end.
The UCC allows proper consumer disclaimers; other law limits them.
It may never have become part of the contract, and other law may void it.
Several other routes exist, including § 2-207 and Magnuson-Moss.
topic: Wks 5–7 · Variation by agreement & disclaimers — Consumer buyer
pre: An experienced commercial fisherman tells a dealer his boat's size and weight; on the dealer's recommendation, he buys a diesel engine. At delivery, he signs the dealer's standard receipt, which says on the back in large capitals: “SELLER DISCLAIMS ALL IMPLIED WARRANTIES, INCLUDING MERCHANTABILITY.” The engine smokes constantly and is underpowered for the boat. What is the fisherman's best argument?

q: On the course's continuum between freedom of contract and paternalism, which transaction calls for the MOST protection against warranty disclaimers?
o: A consumer's purchase of prepackaged new consumer goods.
A merchant's purchase of specially made commercial goods built to its specs.
A merchant-to-merchant sale of commercial goods.
A sale of used goods between businesses.
oe: Correct. The continuum runs from specially made commercial goods and merchant-to-merchant deals (most freedom of contract) through used goods to prepackaged new consumer goods (most protection).
That's the freedom-of-contract end.
That's toward the freedom end.
Used goods sit in the middle.
topic: Wks 5–7 · Variation by agreement & disclaimers — The protection continuum

q: A pawnbroker sells a car “as is, with all faults.” The car turns out to have been stolen, and the owner reclaims it. The buyer sues for breach of the warranty of title. What result?
o: The buyer likely wins: “as is” doesn't disclaim title.
The pawnbroker wins: “as is” excludes all warranties.
The pawnbroker wins: pawnbrokers' sales are like sheriffs' sales.
The buyer wins only if the pawnbroker knew the car was stolen.
oe: Correct. Section 2-312(2). The title warranty isn't designated an “implied” warranty, so § 2-316 doesn't apply (§ 2-312 cmt. 6; Ulbrich v. Groth; Hagerty v. Luxury Asset Capital).
It excludes implied warranties under § 2-316(3)(a), and title isn't one.
Comment 5's circumstances involve sheriffs, executors, and the like, not pawnbrokers' ordinary sales.
Title warranty liability doesn't depend on knowledge.
topic: Wks 5–7 · Variation by agreement & disclaimers — Title disclaimers

q: Which sale most likely carries no warranty of title, even though nothing is said about title?
o: A storage-unit auction of a defaulting tenant's abandoned contents.
A used-car dealer's ordinary sale of a trade-in.
An Article 9 secured party's foreclosure sale of repossessed equipment, with no disclaimer.
A consumer's garage-sale sale of her own bicycle.
oe: Correct. Circumstances that give the buyer reason to know the seller sells only such right as it or a third party may have disclaim the title warranty (§ 2-312(2); cmt. 5: sheriffs, executors, certain foreclosing lienors). Problem 5-5(b) adds storage-unit and warehouse-lien sales. But an Article 9 secured party's disposition includes title warranties unless properly excluded (§ 9-610).
Nothing about an ordinary dealer sale signals a limited title.
Article 9 dispositions include title warranties unless properly excluded.
All sellers, including consumers, warrant title.
topic: Wks 5–7 · Variation by agreement & disclaimers — Circumstances disclaiming title

q: Why might a buyer sensibly agree to an express disclaimer of the warranty of title outside a sheriff's sale?
o: Ownership is uncertain, and the price reflects the risk.
Because title disclaimers also eliminate the seller's liability for defects.
Because the warranty of title protects only merchants.
Because disclaiming title makes the sale exempt from Article 2.
oe: Correct. Problem 5-5(a): a quitclaim-type sale makes sense when provenance is uncertain and the price reflects the buyer's assumption of the risk.
A title disclaimer doesn't affect quality warranties.
All buyers get it; it's made by all sellers.
A title disclaimer doesn't change scope.
topic: Wks 5–7 · Variation by agreement & disclaimers — Agreeing to a title disclaimer

q: A seller wants to reduce its exposure for defective goods. Its lawyer explains the difference between disclaiming warranties and limiting remedies. Which statement is correct?
o: A disclaimer can mean no breach; a limitation restricts damages after breach.
The two are the same; both are governed by § 2-316.
Remedy limitations must be conspicuous, but disclaimers need not be.
A remedy limitation is implied in every contract unless the buyer objects.
oe: Correct. In the formula “contract + breach + damages + causation,” disclaimers attack contract and breach, while limitations attack damages. Sections 2-312 and 2-316 govern disclaimers; §§ 2-718 and 2-719 (plus unconscionability) govern limitations, which are never implied by law.
Section 2-316(4) points to §§ 2-718 and 2-719 for remedy limits, which are a separate category.
It's roughly the reverse: certain disclaimers must be conspicuous; remedy limitations need not be.
Limitations are never implied; they must be in the agreement.
topic: Wks 6–7 · Remedies & remedy limits — Disclaimer vs. limitation

q: A bakery receives a defective commercial mixer. It pays $400 to have a technician inspect it, $300 to store it pending return, and loses $12,000 in profits on customer orders while it lacks a working mixer; the seller knew at contracting that the bakery depended on the mixer to fill orders and the bakery couldn't reasonably avoid the loss. How are these losses classified?
o: Inspection and storage are incidental; lost profits are consequential.
All three are consequential damages.
All three are incidental damages.
The lost profits aren't recoverable, because profits are always too speculative.
oe: Correct. Incidental damages (§ 2-715(1)) are reasonable expenses of responding to the breach, such as inspection, transportation, storage, and costs of cover. Consequential damages (§ 2-715(2)) include losses from requirements the seller had reason to know of that the buyer couldn't reasonably prevent, and injury to person or property caused by breach of warranty.
Inspection and storage costs are incidental.
Lost profits from the buyer's operations are consequential.
Consequential losses the seller had reason to know of are recoverable if proven.
topic: Wks 6–7 · Remedies & remedy limits — Incidental vs. consequential

q: A seller repudiates a contract to sell 1,000 tons of steel at $500 per ton. The buyer promptly buys substitute steel in good faith at $560 per ton. The market price at the time the buyer learned of the breach was $550. What is the buyer's most natural measure of damages?
o: Cover minus contract, $60 per ton, plus incidental damages.
Market price minus contract price, $50 per ton, which is the only measure available.
The full $560 per ton the buyer paid for the substitute steel.
Value as warranted minus value as accepted.
oe: Correct. After repudiation or non-delivery, the buyer may cancel, recover any price paid, and either cover (§ 2-712, cover minus contract) or recover market minus contract (§ 2-713), plus damages under § 2-715. Specific performance is available only in limited circumstances (§ 2-716).
Cover is an alternative the buyer may choose.
The buyer recovers the difference from the contract price, not the full cover price.
That measure applies to accepted nonconforming goods (§ 2-714).
topic: Wks 6–7 · Remedies & remedy limits — Buyer's remedies after non-delivery

q: A buyer accepts a used delivery truck warranted to have a rebuilt engine. The engine turns out not to be rebuilt. As warranted, the truck would have been worth $40,000; as delivered, it's worth $31,000. The contract price was $38,000. The buyer gave timely notice. What is the buyer's basic recovery?
o: $9,000: value as warranted minus value as accepted.
$7,000, the contract price minus the value as accepted.
The full $38,000, because the buyer may return the truck at any time.
Nothing, because by accepting the truck the buyer waived the breach.
oe: Correct. A buyer who accepts must pay the price but may recover for the nonconformity (§§ 2-607(1), 2-714(2)): value as warranted minus value as accepted, at the time and place of acceptance.
The measure uses the value as warranted, not the contract price.
Return requires a proper revocation of acceptance under § 2-608.
Acceptance doesn't impair remedies if the buyer gives timely notice.
topic: Wks 6–7 · Remedies & remedy limits — Accepted nonconforming goods

q: A buyer repudiates a contract to buy 500 custom cabinets for $100,000 before delivery. The seller, acting in a commercially reasonable way, resells the cabinets to another buyer for $85,000 and spends $2,000 on resale costs. What can the seller most naturally recover?
o: $15,000 (contract price minus resale price) plus $2,000 in incidental damages.
The full $100,000 contract price, because the buyer repudiated.
Only $2,000, because the seller avoided most of the loss by reselling.
$15,000, but not the resale costs, which the seller must absorb.
oe: Correct. When the buyer repudiates, the seller may withhold delivery, cancel, and recover damages: resale (§ 2-706), market (§ 2-708(1)), or lost profit (§ 2-708(2)), plus incidental damages (§ 2-710). If the buyer had prepaid, it would get restitution less the seller's damages (§ 2-718(2)).
An action for the price (§ 2-709) is generally for accepted goods or goods that can't reasonably be resold.
The difference between contract and resale price is recoverable too.
Incidental damages, including resale costs, are recoverable under § 2-710.
topic: Wks 6–7 · Remedies & remedy limits — Seller's remedies

q: A seller delivers goods on credit. Eight days after the buyer receives them, the seller learns the buyer was insolvent at the time of delivery. The buyer made no written representation of solvency. Can the seller get the goods back?
o: Yes, if it demands reclamation within ten days after the buyer's receipt.
No: once goods are delivered on credit, the seller's only remedy is to sue for the price.
Yes, at any time within three months of delivery.
Only if the seller had reserved a security interest.
oe: Correct. Section 2-702(2) allows reclamation from a buyer who received goods on credit while insolvent if the seller demands within ten days of receipt. The ten-day limit doesn't apply if the buyer made a written misrepresentation of solvency within three months before delivery.
Section 2-702(2) provides a limited reclamation right.
The three-month window relates to written misrepresentations of solvency; otherwise the limit is ten days.
Reclamation under § 2-702(2) doesn't require a security interest.
topic: Wks 6–7 · Remedies & remedy limits — Reclamation from an insolvent buyer

q: A bakery orders a custom oven for delivery by September 1, telling the manufacturer about its planned expansion and that time is of the essence. After discussing profit margins, the parties negotiate a “liquidated damages” clause of $1,000 per day of delay. The oven arrives a month late. The manufacturer proves September was slow and the bakery would have earned only $2,500. Is the $30,000 clause enforceable?
o: Likely yes, if reasonable when made, though actual harm invites a penalty argument.
No: liquidated damages can never exceed the actual loss.
Yes, automatically, because commercial parties negotiated it.
No, because liquidated-damages clauses must be conspicuous.
oe: Correct. The disjunctive “or” lets a clause reasonable at contracting stand even if actual harm proves smaller. Courts split on how much weight actual harm gets; the stronger view upholds a clause reasonable when made (Problem 5-6).
The statute allows reasonableness in light of anticipated harm.
Even negotiated clauses must be reasonable; an unreasonably large amount is a void penalty.
Nothing requires an LD clause to be conspicuous.
topic: Wks 6–7 · Remedies & remedy limits — Liquidated damages

q: A contract fixes liquidated damages for the seller's total non-delivery of a $2 million machine at $100. What is the most likely treatment of this clause?
o: It may be stricken as unconscionable for being too small.
It's void as a penalty.
It's enforceable, because liquidated damages need only be reasonable in light of actual harm.
It's enforceable, because § 2-718 limits only clauses that favor the buyer.
oe: Correct. Section 2-718(1) voids unreasonably large amounts as penalties; comment 1 notes an unreasonably small amount may be stricken as unconscionable.
Penalties are unreasonably large amounts.
An absurdly small figure isn't reasonable in light of any harm.
Section 2-718 applies to damages for breach by either party.
topic: Wks 6–7 · Remedies & remedy limits — Unreasonably small

q: A buyer pays a $1,500 deposit on a $5,000 sofa and then wrongfully repudiates. The contract has no liquidated-damages clause, and the seller can't prove any actual damages. How much of the deposit must the seller return?
o: $1,000: the seller keeps $500.
$500: the seller may keep 20% of the total price.
Nothing: a breaching buyer forfeits its deposit.
The full $1,500, because the seller proved no damages.
oe: Correct. Section 2-718(2)(b): absent an LD clause, the buyer gets restitution of the amount by which its payments exceed the smaller of 20% of the value of its total performance or $500, subject to offset for the seller's proven damages.
The seller keeps the smaller of 20% or $500.
Article 2 limits forfeiture of deposits.
The seller may keep the statutory amount even without proving damages.
topic: Wks 6–7 · Remedies & remedy limits — Deposits

q: A manufacturer's warranty states: “Seller will repair or replace defective parts.” It doesn't say this remedy is exclusive. A defect causes losses the buyer seeks to recover as ordinary damages. Is the buyer limited to repair or replacement?
o: No: agreed remedies are optional unless expressly agreed to be exclusive.
Yes: any remedy stated in the contract is the buyer's sole remedy.
Yes, if the clause is conspicuous.
No, because repair-or-replace remedies are unenforceable in sales of goods.
oe: Correct. Section 2-719(1)(b); comment 2 presumes clauses are cumulative, so exclusivity must be clearly expressed. Like § 2-718, § 2-719 doesn't require conspicuousness.
Without clear exclusivity, the remedy is merely an additional option.
Conspicuousness isn't the test; exclusivity is.
They're enforceable; this one just isn't exclusive.
topic: Wks 6–7 · Remedies & remedy limits — Exclusive remedies

q: A tractor's warranty makes repair or replacement of defective parts the buyer's exclusive remedy. The tractor sits in the dealer's shop for over a year while the dealer repeatedly fails to fix a hydraulic defect. What may the buyer now recover?
o: Ordinary UCC remedies, because the exclusive remedy has failed of its essential purpose.
Only repair or replacement, because the buyer agreed that remedy would be exclusive.
Only a refund of the price, as a substitute exclusive remedy.
Nothing, unless the buyer proves the dealer acted in bad faith.
oe: Correct. Section 2-719(2): when circumstances cause an exclusive or limited remedy to fail of its essential purpose, remedy may be had as provided in the Code. Comment 1 insists on at least a fair quantum of remedy (Adams v. J.I. Case).
An exclusive remedy that fails of its essential purpose gives way.
The buyer gets the Code's ordinary remedies, not a court-made substitute.
Repeated failure to repair within a reasonable time is enough; bad faith isn't required.
topic: Wks 6–7 · Remedies & remedy limits — Failure of essential purpose

q: Which limited remedy is LEAST likely to fail of its essential purpose?
o: A refund-or-repair remedy from a solvent seller that promptly fixes the defect on the first attempt.
A store-credit-only remedy from a retailer that has since gone out of business.
A “replace defective parts only” remedy when a single defective part destroyed the entire machine.
A 30-day replacement period for a defect that can't be discovered until month six.
oe: Correct. The remedy did its job. Problem 5-7 examples of failure include a store credit from a retailer that goes bankrupt, repeated failed repairs, replacement of a part when the defect destroyed the whole machine, and a replacement period that expires before a latent defect can be found.
The worthless credit fails of its essential purpose.
Replacing the part is useless, so the remedy fails.
The remedy expires before it can be used.
topic: Wks 6–7 · Remedies & remedy limits — Scenarios of failure

q: Two sales contracts exclude consequential damages. In the first, a consumer's new space heater explodes, burning the buyer. In the second, a defective industrial dryer halts a factory, causing lost profits. How will courts likely treat the exclusions?
o: The first is prima facie unconscionable; the second isn't.
Both are void, because consequential damages can never be excluded.
Both are valid, because consequential damages can always be excluded.
The first is valid and the second is void, because businesses can't waive lost profits.
oe: Correct. Section 2-719(3). The consumer presumption is rebuttable (Problem 5-8: e.g., a bargained-for lower price with assumed risk and warnings). Article 2 doesn't define personal injury, so other law does.
They may be excluded unless unconscionable.
