Personal-injury exclusions in consumer sales are prima facie unconscionable.
Commercial-loss exclusions aren't presumptively unconscionable.
topic: Wks 6–7 · Remedies & remedy limits — Consequential exclusions

q: A new-car warranty limits remedies to repair or replacement and separately excludes consequential damages. The dealer can't fix a recurring no-start problem, and the limited remedy fails of its essential purpose. The warranty booklet was in the glove compartment, and there's no evidence the buyer saw it before signing. Under Razor v. Hyundai, what happens to the consequential-damages exclusion?
o: It stands on its own, but here it's unconscionable.
It automatically falls because the limited remedy failed.
It survives because it was printed in clear capital letters.
It survives because unconscionability can be judged only from the face of the clause.
oe: Correct. Illinois adopted the majority independent approach (Chatlos v. NCR): “two concentric layers of protection.” A limitation given after the sale is ineffective, so the exclusion was unconscionable; damages run under § 2-714(2).
That's the dependent approach (Adams v. J.I. Case), which Razor rejected.
Clear type is irrelevant if the buyer couldn't see the term before contracting.
Razor considered the circumstances, including when the warranty became available.
topic: Wks 6–7 · Remedies & remedy limits — Razor v. Hyundai

q: Which criticism did the dissent from the denial of rehearing in Razor v. Hyundai raise?
o: That the holding burdens manufacturers and is inconsistent.
The court should have adopted the dependent approach.
Consumers should never be bound by consequential-damages exclusions.
The jury, not the court, should decide unconscionability.
oe: Correct. Justice McMorrow agreed with the independent approach but objected to how the majority applied unconscionability.
The dissent agreed with the independent approach.
The dissent defended the exclusion's enforceability.
Unconscionability is a question of law; the dissent didn't dispute that.
topic: Wks 6–7 · Remedies & remedy limits — Razor's dissent

q: Clause A: “Seller shall pay Buyer $500 per day of late delivery.” Clause B: “Seller's liability shall not exceed $5,000.” How do these clauses differ?
o: A is liquidated damages; B is a cap on proven damages.
Both are liquidated-damages clauses tested by § 2-718.
Both are caps tested by § 2-719.
Clause A is a cap and Clause B is liquidated damages.
oe: Correct. Problem 5-9: LD fixes the amount regardless of actual loss (higher or lower); a cap or limited remedy restricts categories or amounts but requires proof of actual loss.
A cap doesn't fix the amount; it limits recovery of proven damages.
A per-day amount payable regardless of actual loss is liquidated damages.
It's the reverse.
topic: Wks 6–7 · Remedies & remedy limits — LD vs. cap

q: A contract signed in 2018 states: “Any action for breach of warranty may be brought within six years.” The goods were tendered in March 2019. The buyer discovers a latent defect in 2024 and sues in May 2024. The warranty didn't explicitly extend to future performance. Is the suit timely?
o: No: the period can't be extended and ran from tender.
Yes: the parties agreed to a six-year period, and freedom of contract lets them set it.
Yes, because the limitations period began when the buyer discovered the defect in 2024.
Yes, because the four-year period runs from the date of the breach suit's first demand letter.
oe: Correct. Section 2-725(1): four years from accrual; the original agreement may reduce it to not less than one year but may not extend it. Accrual is at tender (§ 2-725(2)) unless the warranty explicitly extends to future performance, in which case it accrues on discovery.
Section 2-725(1) forbids extending the period.
Discovery accrual applies only to warranties explicitly extending to future performance.
The period runs from accrual, which for warranty claims is tender of delivery.
topic: Wks 6–7 · Remedies & remedy limits — Statute of limitations

q: Which statement correctly distinguishes the parol evidence rule from the statute of frauds?
o: The SOF concerns enforceability; the PER concerns which terms come in.
Both rules bar enforcement of any agreement not in writing.
The PER applies only to contracts for $500 or more.
The statute of frauds governs prior agreements, while the PER governs future modifications.
oe: Correct. SOF problems arise when there's no signed record; PER problems arise only when a record adopted by both exists. If the SOF isn't met, the agreement is unenforceable; if the PER excludes a term, the rest of the agreement is still enforceable.
The PER is about admissibility of evidence of terms, not enforceability.
The $500 threshold belongs to the statute of frauds.
Neither statement is right; NOM clauses govern future modifications.
topic: Wks 6–8 · Parol evidence rule — PER vs. statute of frauds

q: A contract contains: “This Agreement may not be modified except by a writing signed by both parties.” A party argues this clause bars evidence of an oral agreement made the day before signing. Is that right?
o: No: it's a NOM clause about future changes, not a merger clause.
Yes: any clause requiring writings bars all oral evidence.
Yes, because NOM clauses and merger clauses are interchangeable.
No, because NOM clauses are unenforceable under the UCC.
oe: Correct. Problem 5-11, clause 4: a NOM clause operates under § 2-209(2) on later changes; merger clauses concern prior and contemporaneous agreements under § 2-202.
A NOM clause doesn't address what came before the writing.
They do different jobs.
They're enforceable under § 2-209(2); they're just not merger clauses.
topic: Wks 6–8 · Parol evidence rule — Merger vs. NOM

q: A fully integrated written contract for machinery has a merger clause. Which evidence is the PER most likely to bar?
o: Evidence that, before signing, the parties orally agreed the seller would also provide free training.
Evidence that, a week after signing, the parties agreed to change the delivery date.
Evidence that the seller fraudulently misrepresented the machine's capacity to induce the signing.
Evidence that the parties agreed the contract wouldn't take effect until the buyer's financing was approved.
oe: Correct. That's a prior additional term offered as part of the agreement, which a complete and exclusive writing bars. The PER doesn't bar evidence of later modifications, fraud or mistake, interpretation of a term, a condition precedent to the agreement's effectiveness, or a separate agreement.
The PER never bars subsequent agreements (though a NOM clause might).
The PER doesn't bar evidence of fraud, even from before execution.
Conditions precedent to the agreement's effectiveness fall outside the PER.
topic: Wks 6–8 · Parol evidence rule — When the PER doesn't apply

q: A signed purchase order states the price, quantity, and delivery date for 500 chairs and says nothing else. It has no merger clause. The buyer offers evidence of a prior oral agreement that the seller would deliver the chairs assembled, a term the order doesn't address. Assume the court finds the writing final but not complete and exclusive. Is the evidence admissible?
o: Yes: consistent additional terms come in under a partial integration.
No: once there's a final writing, no prior oral terms may be considered.
No, because prior oral agreements are always inadmissible.
Yes, and the evidence would be admissible even if it contradicted the price term.
oe: Correct. Under § 2-202(b), consistent additional terms come in unless the writing was intended as complete and exclusive. Assembly arguably supplements rather than contradicts.
A partially integrated writing bars only contradictory terms.
Prior oral supplementary terms are admissible with a partial integration.
Contradictory prior terms are barred for any final writing.
topic: Wks 6–8 · Parol evidence rule — Classifying the writing

q: Midway through negotiations, a buyer sends a draft term sheet that both parties treat as tentative; it's never adopted as final on any term. The seller offers evidence of an oral agreement on warranty terms made later in the talks. Does the PER bar it?
o: No: a tentative draft isn't a final writing.
Yes: any signed writing bars evidence of oral terms.
Yes, because the warranty terms should have been in the draft.
No, but only because the warranty term is a contemporaneous writing.
oe: Correct. A non-final writing doesn't trigger the rule. (Even a document generated mid-negotiation can be final as to the terms it adopts, if both parties intend that.)
Finality, not signature alone, triggers the PER.
The “certainly would have been included” test applies to final writings.
The evidence is oral, and the reason it's admissible is the writing's lack of finality.
topic: Wks 6–8 · Parol evidence rule — Unfinished writings

q: A writing is complete and exclusive. Which of the following evidence is admissible?
o: Usage-of-trade evidence that supplements the writing.
A prior oral agreement adding a consistent term.
A prior written side letter adding a consistent term.
A contemporaneous oral agreement adding a consistent term.
oe: Correct. Under the chart, a complete and exclusive writing bars all prior oral and written terms and contemporaneous oral terms, whether supplementary or contradictory. Course of dealing, usage of trade, and course of performance may still explain or supplement (§ 2-202(a)).
Complete integration bars consistent additional prior terms.
Prior written terms are barred by a complete integration too.
Contemporaneous oral terms are barred as well.
topic: Wks 6–8 · Parol evidence rule — The PER chart

q: At closing, the parties sign a final but not complete purchase agreement and, at the same meeting, a separate signed letter stating that the seller will provide spare parts for five years. Is the letter barred by the PER?
o: No: § 2-202 doesn't bar contemporaneous writings.
Yes: all writings other than the final contract are excluded.
Yes, because it adds a term the main contract doesn't mention.
No, but only if the letter is signed by a notary.
oe: Correct. That's the tricky chart cell: contemporaneous written terms aren't barred. For a complete and exclusive record, such a writing is simply part of the integrated record (“N/A” on the chart).
Section 2-202 doesn't bar contemporaneous writings.
Supplementary terms aren't barred by a partial integration in any event.
No such formality exists.
topic: Wks 6–8 · Parol evidence rule — Contemporaneous writings

q: A complete and exclusive written contract, with a merger clause, says “delivery within 30 days.” The seller offers evidence of usage of trade that “30 days” in the industry means 30 business days. The buyer argues the court must first find the term ambiguous. Which is correct?
o: Admissible to explain, with no ambiguity threshold.
The evidence is barred, because the merger clause excludes all extrinsic evidence.
The evidence is admissible only if the court first finds “30 days” ambiguous.
The evidence is admissible and automatically controls over the express term.
oe: Correct. Comment 1(c) rejects an ambiguity threshold for course of dealing, usage of trade, and course of performance. They explain or supplement even complete writings unless carefully negated (cmt. 2). Contradiction is governed by § 1-303(e).
Merger clauses don't exclude usage unless it's carefully negated.
Comment 1(c) rejects that threshold for these sources.
Express terms prevail if the two can't reasonably be reconciled.
topic: Wks 6–8 · Parol evidence rule — Course of dealing and usage

q: Which clause most effectively establishes that a writing is a complete and exclusive statement of the parties' agreement?
o: “This is the complete and exclusive statement of our agreement.”
“This Agreement represents the final agreement of the parties.”
“This Agreement supersedes all prior agreements, written or oral.”
“This Agreement may not be modified except by a writing signed by both parties.”
oe: Correct. Problem 5-11, clause 2, tracks § 2-202(b)'s language. A merger clause is highly probative of full integration but not conclusive.
“Final” tracks only partial integration; it bars contradiction but not consistent additional terms.
Helpful but incomplete: it doesn't address contemporaneous oral agreements or say the writing is complete and exclusive. Best combined with clause 2.
That's a NOM clause about future modifications.
topic: Wks 6–8 · Parol evidence rule — Merger clauses

q: A two-page form contract between a consumer and a dealer contains a boilerplate merger clause. The consumer offers evidence of a prior oral agreement on a term the form doesn't address. How do courts approach whether the writing is complete and exclusive?
o: It's probative, not conclusive, and courts differ on what to consider.
A merger clause conclusively establishes complete integration.
Merger clauses are ignored in consumer contracts.
The jury decides, based on whether the consumer read the clause.
oe: Correct. Comment 3: if the term, had it been agreed, would certainly have been included in the document, evidence of it must be kept from the trier of fact. Scholars suspect judges who believe the evidence tend to find the writing incomplete (Apex LLC).
It's strong evidence, not conclusive.
Nothing in § 2-202 says so, though courts may be skeptical of boilerplate.
Integration is generally a question for the court.
topic: Wks 6–8 · Parol evidence rule — Merger clause not conclusive

q: Courts use several tests to decide whether a proffered term supplements or contradicts a final writing. Which test is NOT one of them?
o: Whether the party offering the evidence is a merchant.
Whether the term directly contradicts or negates a term in the writing.
Whether the term lacks reasonable harmony with the writing.
Whether the term is one that might naturally be omitted from the writing.
oe: Correct. Merchant status plays no role. The tests: (i) direct contradiction or negation of a term; (ii) absence of reasonable harmony with the writing (Alaska Northern); (iii) whether the parties would certainly have included the term if agreed (cmt. 3); (iv) whether it's a term that might naturally be omitted (Restatement § 216).
That's the narrowest test.
That's the Alaska Northern test.
That's Restatement § 216.
topic: Wks 6–8 · Parol evidence rule — Supplement vs. contradict

q: A buyer gets a court to admit usage-of-trade evidence over a PER objection. Which statement is most accurate?
o: It still must prove the usage and persuade the fact-finder.
The buyer wins on that issue, because admitted evidence is conclusive.
The seller may now introduce any prior oral agreements in response.
The writing is now treated as non-final.
oe: Correct. Getting past the PER only gets the evidence to the fact-finder. The proponent bears the burden of proving course of dealing or usage (§ 1-201(b)(8)) and must give § 1-303(g) notice. Courts may treat usage as supplemental more readily because it can be proved by others in the trade (Nanakuli Paving).
Admissibility isn't the same as proof.
Admitting usage doesn't open the door to barred prior agreements.
Admitting usage doesn't change the writing's classification.
topic: Wks 6–8 · Parol evidence rule — Past the PER isn't winning

q: For years, Salem Carpet bought specialized carpet fiber from Fiber Industries using purchase orders and acknowledgments that each said the form “shall constitute the complete and exclusive agreement.” When Fiber phases out the fiber, Salem offers evidence that in the fiber industry, a manufacturer of specialized fiber supplies it for the market life of the buyer's carpet style. The forms are silent on this. Is the evidence admissible?
o: Yes: usage may supplement even a complete writing.
No: the merger clause bars all evidence outside the forms.
No, because usage can explain but never supplement a complete writing.
Yes, but only if the court first finds the forms ambiguous.
oe: Correct. Problem 5-12(a): § 2-202(a). Salem must give notice (§ 1-303(g)), prove the usage, and it must be construed consistently with express terms if reasonable.
A merger clause doesn't negate usage of trade.
Section 2-202(a) allows both explanation and supplementation.
There's no ambiguity threshold for usage.
topic: Wks 6–8 · Parol evidence rule — Salem Carpet: usage

q: Variation: Instead of usage, Salem offers evidence that in earlier discussions, Fiber orally agreed to supply the fiber for the market life of Salem's carpet styles. The forms are silent. Is the evidence admissible?
o: No: prior oral terms are barred by a complete writing.
Yes: it's consistent with the forms, which are silent on the issue.
Yes, because it's the same content as the admissible usage evidence.
No, unless Salem proves fraud.
oe: Correct. Problem 5-12(b): § 2-202(b). And a term this important would certainly have been included (cmt. 3).
Consistency only matters for partially integrated writings.
The source matters: usage comes in; prior oral agreements don't.
Fraud would be a separate route around the PER, but the oral term itself is barred.
topic: Wks 6–8 · Parol evidence rule — Salem Carpet: prior oral agreement
pre: For years, Salem Carpet bought specialized carpet fiber from Fiber Industries using purchase orders and acknowledgments that each said the form “shall constitute the complete and exclusive agreement.” When Fiber phases out the fiber, Salem offers evidence that in the fiber industry, a manufacturer of specialized fiber supplies it for the market life of the buyer's carpet style. The forms are silent on this. Is the evidence admissible?

q: Salem's purchase order included a term that Fiber would “support the integration of all materials supplied into the carpet manufactured by the buyer.” Salem offers (1) usage-of-trade evidence of what that phrase means, and (2) evidence of prior oral discussions explaining what the parties meant. Which is admissible?
o: Usage, yes; prior discussions depend on the jurisdiction.
Both are clearly admissible everywhere.
Neither, because the writing is complete and exclusive.
Only the prior discussions, because usage can't explain a term the parties drafted themselves.
oe: Correct. Problem 5-12(c)(1)–(2): usage explains without an ambiguity threshold (cmt. 1(c)). Explanation isn't contradiction or supplementation, so many courts admit prior negotiations to interpret; some require a finding of ambiguity first.
Courts divide on prior discussions offered to explain.
Interpretation evidence isn't barred the same way, and usage comes in regardless.
Usage can explain the meaning of any term.
topic: Wks 6–8 · Parol evidence rule — Explaining a term

q: During a test drive, a used-car dealer's agent says the four-year-old SUV has never been in an accident and that the dealer will fix it free if it breaks down within 30 days. The buyer signs a writing that says: “WARRANTIES. Buyer is buying the goods AS IS, WHERE IS. Seller makes no warranty, express or implied.” The SUV breaks down in three weeks, and records show major accident repairs. The dealer moves for summary judgment on the warranty claims. What is the dealer's best argument?
o: The PER bars oral warranties that contradict a final writing.
The oral statements were puffing, so no warranties were made.
Express warranties can always be disclaimed by a conspicuous written clause.
“As is” disclaims all warranties, including express ones.
oe: Correct. Problem 5-13: § 2-316(1) makes an irreconcilable disclaimer inoperative, but that's “subject to” § 2-202. Contradiction is barred whether the writing is partially or fully integrated. “As is” disclaims the implied warranties.
“Never been in an accident” is a factual affirmation and “will fix it” is a promise; both are warranties if admissible.
Under § 2-316(1), irreconcilable disclaimers are inoperative; the dealer needs the PER.
“As is” addresses implied warranties.
topic: Wks 6–8 · Parol evidence rule — Oral warranties vs. written disclaimer

q: Same facts. Which is the buyer's strongest response to the dealer's PER argument?
o: The PER doesn't bar evidence of fraud.
The PER never applies to consumer transactions.
Oral warranties always prevail over written disclaimers.
The dealer's motion fails because the writing lacks a merger clause.
oe: Correct. Other arguments: the form wasn't intended as final on warranties; consumer-protection statutes; Restatement of Consumer Contracts § 8 (though it can't override § 2-202). The text calls using the PER to exclude express warranties “potentially very problematic.”
The PER applies to consumer sales, though courts may be skeptical of standard forms.
That's true under § 2-316(1) only if the oral warranties get past the PER.
Contradiction is barred even for a partially integrated writing.
topic: Wks 6–8 · Parol evidence rule — Buyer's best counterarguments
pre: During a test drive, a used-car dealer's agent says the four-year-old SUV has never been in an accident and that the dealer will fix it free if it breaks down within 30 days. The buyer signs a writing that says: “WARRANTIES. Buyer is buying the goods AS IS, WHERE IS. Seller makes no warranty, express or implied.” The SUV breaks down in three weeks, and records show major accident repairs. The dealer moves for summary judgment on the warranty claims. What is the dealer's best argument?

q: A steel distributor contracts to sell 100 standard steel I-beams to a builder. Without asking the builder, the distributor arranges for a mill to deliver the beams directly. The mill tenders conforming beams late, and the builder sues the distributor. The distributor argues it was relieved of liability when it delegated. What result?
o: Permitted, but the distributor remains liable.
The delegation was invalid, because the builder didn't consent.
The distributor is relieved of liability, because the mill assumed the duty.
The builder must sue the mill, because the mill performed.
oe: Correct. Section 2-210(1): a party may perform through a delegate unless otherwise agreed or the other party has a substantial interest in having the original promisor perform. The delegator stays on the hook absent a novation.
The counter-party's consent isn't required for delegation.
Delegation never releases the delegator absent a novation.
The builder may sue the distributor, which remains liable.
topic: Wk 8 · Assignment & delegation — Delegation of a seller's duty

q: A company commissions a sculptor-fabricator to design and build a custom bronze installation, subject to the company's approval of a prototype. The fabricator delegates the work to an unrelated foundry. Must the company accept the foundry's performance?
o: Likely not, given its substantial interest in the original promisor.
Yes: delegation is always permitted unless the contract prohibits it.
Yes, as long as the foundry is equally skilled.
No, because sellers may never delegate their duties.
oe: Correct. Section 2-210(1). Buyers are far more likely than sellers to have such an interest, because quality depends on who makes the goods (Problem 6-2(G)).
The substantial-interest limit applies even without a contractual prohibition.
The question is the obligee's substantial interest in the original promisor's performance.
Sellers generally may delegate; the custom nature of this work is the problem.
topic: Wk 8 · Assignment & delegation — Substantial interest

q: A seller contracts to sell steel beams to a buyer for $20,000, F.O.B. seller's yard. The seller assigns its right to payment to a bank, and the bank notifies the buyer and instructs it to pay the bank. The seller tenders conforming beams, and the buyer accepts. The buyer then pays the seller. Has the buyer discharged its obligation?
o: No: after notice, only payment to the bank discharges it.
Yes: the buyer's contract is with the seller, so paying the seller always discharges it.
Yes, because the buyer never consented to the assignment.
No, and the buyer also loses its defenses against the seller.
oe: Correct. Section 9-406(a). Assigning the right to payment doesn't materially change the buyer's duty (§ 2-210(2)–(3)), and the buyer keeps any defenses it had against the seller (Problem 6-2(a)).
After notice, payment to the assignor doesn't discharge.
No consent is needed to assign a right to payment.
The buyer keeps its defenses, such as nonconformity.
topic: Wk 8 · Assignment & delegation — Assigning the right to payment

q: Variation: The contract says, “Assignment is prohibited, and any attempted assignment is void.” The seller assigns its right to payment to the bank anyway, and the bank notifies the buyer. Must the buyer pay the bank?
o: Yes: anti-assignment terms don't bind rights to payment.
No: the clause expressly makes any assignment void.
No, but the seller is liable to the buyer for breaching the clause.
Yes, but only if the buyer had already accepted the beams.
oe: Correct. Section 9-406(d) reflects a strong policy favoring free alienability of receivables, which sellers use to finance their businesses (§ 2-210 cmt. 3; Problem 6-2(b)).
Article 9 overrides the clause as to rights to payment.
The assignment isn't even a breach under § 9-406(d).
Acceptance doesn't affect whether the anti-assignment term is effective.
topic: Wk 8 · Assignment & delegation — Anti-assignment clause and accounts
pre: A seller contracts to sell steel beams to a buyer for $20,000, F.O.B. seller's yard. The seller assigns its right to payment to a bank, and the bank notifies the buyer and instructs it to pay the bank. The seller tenders conforming beams, and the buyer accepts. The buyer then pays the seller. Has the buyer discharged its obligation?

q: The seller assigns “the contract” for 100 steel I-beams to a manufacturer, which accepts. The manufacturer tenders conforming beams. Must the buyer accept them, and whom must it pay?
o: Accept and pay the manufacturer; the seller remains liable.
The buyer may refuse the beams, because it contracted with the seller, not the manufacturer.
The buyer must accept the beams but must still pay the original seller.
The seller is released from liability once the manufacturer accepts the assignment.
oe: Correct. Section 2-210(5): an assignment of “the contract” is an assignment of rights and, unless indicated otherwise, a delegation of duties, and the assignee's acceptance is a promise to perform. The buyer has no substantial interest in who supplies standard beams. Section 2-210(6) treats the delegation as grounds for insecurity (Problem 6-2(c)).
Delegation is permitted absent a substantial interest or contrary agreement.
The assignee of the right to payment is entitled to payment after notice.
Delegation never releases the delegator.
topic: Wk 8 · Assignment & delegation — Assigning “the contract”

q: A contract says, “Neither party may assign this contract.” The buyer assigns its right to receive the goods to a subsidiary, and the seller argues the assignment violates the clause. How is the clause interpreted?
o: It bars only delegation of duties.
It bars both assigning rights and delegating duties.
It's unenforceable, because rights can always be assigned.
It bars assigning rights but not delegating duties.
oe: Correct. Section 2-210(4). Even language that clearly bars assigning rights may make an assignment only a breach rather than ineffective, unless it also says any attempted assignment is void.
Section 2-210(4) reads it narrowly.
Prohibitions can be effective, but this wording reaches only delegation.
It's the reverse.
topic: Wk 8 · Assignment & delegation — Prohibiting assignment of “the contract”

q: A seller has a requirements contract to supply all the packaging a small bakery needs. The bakery assigns its rights under the contract to a national snack company with requirements 50 times larger. Is the assignment effective?
o: Likely not, because it materially increases the seller's burden.
Yes: rights can always be assigned without consent.
Yes, because requirements must be in good faith, which protects the seller.
No, because requirements contracts can never be assigned.
oe: Correct. Section 2-210(2). The materiality limit most often applies to a buyer's assignment of its right to receive performance, especially in output or requirements contracts where the assignee's needs differ (cmt. 4).
Assignment is limited by materiality.
Good faith doesn't cure a material change in the seller's burden.
They can be, unless the change is material.
topic: Wk 8 · Assignment & delegation — Materiality limit on assignment

q: A contract prohibits assignment. After the seller fully performs, it assigns to a collection firm its right to the unpaid price; separately, a buyer assigns its claim for damages for the seller's breach of the whole contract. Are these assignments effective despite the prohibition?
o: Yes: these rights can be assigned despite the ban.
No: a contractual prohibition bars all assignments.
Only the seller's, because only rights to payment can be assigned.
Only the buyer's, because a seller's rights depend on the buyer's consent.
oe: Correct. Section 2-210(2)'s last sentence.
Section 2-210(2) carves out these rights.
Claims for breach of the whole contract are also assignable.
The seller's right arising from full performance is assignable.
topic: Wk 8 · Assignment & delegation — Assignment of a damages claim

q: With no contractual prohibition, which transfer is most likely to be ineffective?
o: A buyer's delegation of payment where its credit matters.
A seller's assignment of its right to receive payment.
A seller's delegation of its duty to deliver standard, fungible goods.
A buyer's assignment of its right to receive goods F.O.B. seller's place.
oe: Correct. Under the Problem 6-1 chart, delegation by either party is permitted unless the other party has a substantial interest in the original promisor's performance (§ 2-210(1)). Assignment of a seller's right to payment rarely affects the buyer's duties.
That doesn't normally materially affect the buyer (§ 2-210(3)).
Buyers rarely have a substantial interest in who delivers fungible goods.
That minimally changes the seller's duty.
topic: Wk 8 · Assignment & delegation — Assignment chart

q: A seller assigns “the contract” to a manufacturer that will perform the seller's duties, despite a clause stating that “any attempted assignment is void.” The manufacturer argues § 9-406(d) makes the clause ineffective. Is it right?
o: No: Article 9 doesn't cover an assignee that must perform.
Yes: § 9-406(d) invalidates every anti-assignment clause.
Yes, because delegation clauses are always unenforceable.
No, because a “void” clause can never be overridden by statute.
oe: Correct. Section 9-109(d)(6). Ordinary assignment law governs, so the buyer need not accept the manufacturer's performance (Problem 6-2(D)).
It doesn't apply where the assignee must also perform.
Contractual prohibitions on delegation are enforceable.
Section 9-406(d) can override it for pure assignments of accounts.
topic: Wk 8 · Assignment & delegation — Assignee who must also perform

q: Party A ends a supply contract because Party B failed to deliver two installments. Party C ends a different supply contract under a clause allowing either party to end it on 60 days' notice, with no breach involved. Which statement is correct?
o: A cancelled for breach; C terminated without one.
Both terminated, so neither keeps any remedies.
Both cancelled, because each ended the contract early.
C cancelled and A terminated.
oe: Correct. Cancellation (§ 2-106(4)) is a remedy on breach (§§ 2-703(f), 2-711(1)). Termination (§ 2-106(3)) ends the contract for a reason other than breach, usually under a power the agreement creates.
Cancellation preserves remedies for breach.
Cancellation requires the other party's breach.
It's the reverse.
topic: Wk 8 · Termination, insecurity & repudiation — Cancellation vs. termination

q: A shutter manufacturer has supplied a retailer under an agreement with no fixed term for three years. The retailer gives 90 days' notice that it's ending the relationship to switch to a cheaper supplier. The manufacturer argues the retailer can't terminate without a good reason. Under § 2-309 and Santa Fe Custom Shutters v. Home Depot, what result?
o: The retailer may terminate with reasonable notice.
The retailer may not terminate without good cause.
The retailer may terminate without notice, because the contract has no fixed term.
The contract is void for lacking a duration term.
oe: Correct. Section 2-309(2)–(3). Santa Fe held good faith applies to termination but doesn't override the right to terminate “at any time.” Reasonable notice means enough time to arrange substitutes (Coburn Supply).
Santa Fe rejected a good-cause requirement.
Reasonable notification is required except on an agreed event.
Indefinite contracts are valid for a reasonable time and terminable on notice.
topic: Wk 8 · Termination, insecurity & repudiation — Indefinite contracts

q: A distribution agreement says either party may end it “immediately, without notice.” The manufacturer ends it without warning the day after the distributor signs a five-year warehouse lease to handle the product. Which statement is most accurate?
o: The clause fails if its operation is unconscionable.
The clause is always enforceable, because the parties agreed to it.
The clause is always void, because notice can never be waived.
The manufacturer's termination was a repudiation, because termination requires breach.
oe: Correct. Section 2-309(3). Termination except on an agreed event requires reasonable notification, and parties can't waive it where doing so would be unconscionable.
Section 2-309(3) limits such clauses.
It's invalid only if its operation would be unconscionable.
Termination is ending the contract for reasons other than breach.
topic: Wk 8 · Termination, insecurity & repudiation — Dispensing with notice

q: A seller learns facts giving it reasonable grounds to doubt that a buyer will pay. Which step is required before the seller may suspend its own performance under § 2-609?
o: A written demand for adequate assurance.
A phone call to the buyer's chief financial officer.
A court order finding the buyer insolvent.
Thirty days' notice before any demand.
oe: Correct. Section 2-609(1): with reasonable grounds for insecurity, a party may in writing demand adequate assurance and, until it gets it, suspend any performance for which it hasn't already received the agreed return, if commercially reasonable. Failure to respond adequately within a reasonable time not exceeding 30 days is a repudiation (subsection (4)).
An oral demand doesn't give the right to suspend.
No court order is needed.
The 30 days is the buyer's maximum response time after a demand.
topic: Wk 8 · Termination, insecurity & repudiation — Adequate assurance basics

q: Between merchants, how are the reasonableness of grounds for insecurity and the adequacy of an assurance determined, and must the grounds relate to the contract at issue?
o: By commercial standards; grounds may arise elsewhere.
By the demanding party's honest belief, and the grounds must arise from this contract.
By a jury, applying a negligence standard.
By the contract's express terms only.
oe: Correct. Section 2-609(2) and cmt. 3. A purely subjective fear isn't enough. But a buyer who agreed to pay against documents can't evade that risk by demanding assurance.
Reasonableness is objective, and grounds needn't relate to this contract.
Commercial standards govern between merchants.
Section 2-609's standards apply unless validly varied.
topic: Wk 8 · Termination, insecurity & repudiation — Grounds and merchants

q: A grain cooperative has hedge-to-arrive contracts with a farm. The market moves so that delivering would cost the farm heavily, the state attorney general publicly suggests such contracts may be illegal, and the farm stops communicating. The co-op demands payment of margins (or a letter of credit) and a signed promise to deliver. The farm says the demand rewrites the contract. Under Top of Iowa Cooperative v. Sime Farms, which is correct?
o: The grounds were a jury question, and the demand wasn't per se unreasonable.
The demand was a repudiation as a matter of law because it asked for more than the contract required.
The co-op had no grounds, because the farm itself hadn't done anything wrong.
Section 2-609 doesn't apply to agricultural contracts.
oe: Correct. Insecurity needs an objective basis but needn't stem from the other party's own conduct. “All demands for adequate assurance call for more than was originally promised” (White & Summers); § 2-610 cmt. 2.
Top of Iowa rejected that; reasonableness went to the jury.
Grounds can arise from circumstances beyond the party's conduct.
It applies to all contracts for sale.
topic: Wk 8 · Termination, insecurity & repudiation — Top of Iowa

q: A steel supplier, worried about a developer's finances, demands as “adequate assurance” a personal guarantee from the developer's owner, escrowed financing, and an ownership stake in the project. Under the concurrence in Pittsburgh-Des Moines Steel v. Brookhaven Manor, what is the most likely result?
o: It demanded more than adequate assurance as a matter of law.
The demand was proper, because any assurance is adequate if the seller is genuinely worried.
The demand was proper, because Top of Iowa allows any demand for more than the contract requires.
The developer must comply or be in breach immediately.
oe: Correct. The PDM concurrence contrasts with Top of Iowa: a demand for assurance can't be a vehicle to rewrite the deal. An excessive demand may itself be a repudiation.
Adequacy is judged objectively.
Top of Iowa held only that asking for more isn't unreasonable per se.
Failure to respond to a justified demand is a repudiation only after a reasonable time up to 30 days, and this demand likely wasn't justified.
topic: Wk 8 · Termination, insecurity & repudiation — Too much assurance

q: A manufacturer agreed to make goods for a buyer, with installment deliveries and payment 15 days after each delivery. Before the first delivery, it learns Dun & Bradstreet has lowered the buyer's credit rating, the buyer is often late paying suppliers, and it has changed banks amid talk its finances are “extended.” The manufacturer wants to refuse delivery except for cash. What do you advise?
o: Don't demand cash; make a written § 2-609 demand.
Demand cash on delivery, because the buyer's credit rating fell.
Cancel the contract immediately, because the buyer has repudiated.
Deliver on the agreed terms, because insecurity is never grounds for any action.
oe: Correct. Section 2-702(1) allows a cash-only demand only if the buyer is insolvent (generally not paying debts as they come due, unable to pay debts as they come due, or insolvent under bankruptcy law). These facts show credit trouble, not clearly insolvency. Changing the credit term unilaterally risks repudiation (Problem 6-3(a)).
That's allowed only if the buyer is insolvent.
Nothing the buyer has said or done is a repudiation of this contract.
Section 2-609 provides a mechanism to protect the seller.
topic: Wk 8 · Termination, insecurity & repudiation — Unilateral C.O.D.

q: Same facts. The manufacturer sends a written demand for a bank letter of credit and says it will withhold the first delivery until it gets one. The buyer replies that it can pay, refuses the letter of credit as costly and not required, and says it needs timely delivery. Is the buyer's response adequate?
o: Likely inadequate, unless the buyer actually shows solvency.
The response is adequate, because the buyer promised to pay.
The response is inadequate because the buyer refused the specific assurance demanded.
The buyer has repudiated by refusing the letter of credit.
oe: Correct. Comment 4: a promise may suffice from a party of good repute, not a shaky one; a good banker's report can be adequate. Whether demanding a letter of credit is more than adequate is arguable either way (Top of Iowa vs. PDM) (Problem 6-3(b)).
A bare promise from a party with credit problems likely isn't enough.
Adequacy doesn't require exactly what was demanded.
Refusing a possibly excessive demand isn't automatically repudiation.
topic: Wk 8 · Termination, insecurity & repudiation — Letter of credit demand

q: You're drafting a seller's § 2-609 demand letter to a buyer whose credit has deteriorated. Which approach best keeps the demand from being treated as a repudiation?
o: State the grounds, offer alternatives, reserve rights, set a deadline.
Demand a letter of credit only, and state that the contract is cancelled if one isn't provided within five days.
Phone the buyer to express concern, then stop deliveries.
Tell the buyer the seller will deliver only if the buyer agrees to a higher price.
oe: Correct. The slide's model letter: offering options and openness to other assurances keeps the demand adequate rather than excessive.
A single non-negotiable demand with a short deadline risks being excessive and a repudiation.
An oral demand gives no right to suspend.
Conditioning performance on terms beyond the contract is a repudiation.
topic: Wk 8 · Termination, insecurity & repudiation — Drafting the demand letter

q: A giant retailer's form contract says: “Retailer may, whenever it desires, demand from Supplier whatever assurances Retailer deems appropriate and suspend its performance until it receives them.” Is this clause enforceable?
o: Likely not: arbitrary standards are ineffective.
Yes: parties may vary § 2-609 however they like.
Yes, because the retailer has superior bargaining power.
No, because § 2-609 can't be varied in any way.
oe: Correct. Section 2-609 cmt. 6 and § 1-302's limits; compare § 1-309, which requires a good-faith belief for “deems itself insecure” clauses (Problem 6-4, clause 2).
Good faith and reasonableness can't be disclaimed, and arbitrary standards fail.
Bargaining power cuts toward unconscionability, not enforceability.
It can be varied within limits, such as fixing the response time.
topic: Wk 8 · Termination, insecurity & repudiation — Contracting around § 2-609

q: Variation: The same retailer's form also says, “Under no circumstances shall Supplier be entitled to demand adequate assurance or suspend performance.” The supplier had no ability to negotiate. What is the supplier's best argument?
o: It's likely unconscionable and inconsistent with good faith.
The clause is void because § 2-609 can never be waived.
The clause is valid, so the supplier must keep performing even after an outright repudiation.
The clause binds the supplier only if it was conspicuous.
oe: Correct. Problem 6-4, clause 1: arguably a permissible waiver of a protective right, but procedural and substantive unconscionability arguments are strong here.
The rule isn't absolute; the argument is unconscionability and good faith.
The supplier keeps its § 2-610 and § 2-702 rights regardless.
Conspicuousness isn't the test here.
topic: Wk 8 · Termination, insecurity & repudiation — Waiving § 2-609
pre: A giant retailer's form contract says: “Retailer may, whenever it desires, demand from Supplier whatever assurances Retailer deems appropriate and suspend its performance until it receives them.” Is this clause enforceable?

q: Which of the following is a repudiation rather than an ordinary breach?
o: Months early, the seller says it won't ship at all.
On the delivery date, the seller fails to deliver.
The seller asks whether the buyer would consider a price increase.
The buyer pays five days late.
oe: Correct. Repudiation is a clear signal, before performance is due, that a party won't perform (§ 2-610 cmt. 1). Failing to tender when due is a breach, not a repudiation. Failure to give adequate assurance after a justified demand is also a repudiation (§ 2-609(4)).
That's a breach when performance is due.
A request for more isn't itself a repudiation unless performance is conditioned on it.
That's a breach, not a repudiation.
topic: Wk 8 · Termination, insecurity & repudiation — Repudiation vs. breach

q: Before delivery, a seller writes: “Our costs have risen. We'd appreciate it if you would cover the extra $5,000.” In a second scenario, a seller writes: “We will not ship unless you pay an extra $5,000.” Which is a repudiation?
o: Only the second, because it conditions performance.
Both, because each asks for more than the contract requires.
Neither, because price disputes are never repudiations.
Only the first, because it's in writing.
oe: Correct. Section 2-610 cmt. 2.
Asking isn't repudiating; conditioning performance is.
Refusing to perform unless paid more is a repudiation.
Both are in writing; the conditional refusal is the repudiation.
topic: Wk 8 · Termination, insecurity & repudiation — Demands for more

q: A seller repudiates a contract in a way that substantially impairs its value to the buyer. The buyer tells the seller, “We'll wait and hope you reconsider.” Three weeks later, the buyer covers and sues. The seller argues the buyer gave up its remedies by electing to wait. What result?
o: It may still sue, minus avoidable damages from waiting.
The buyer lost its remedies by choosing to wait.
The buyer had to keep performing its own obligations while waiting.
The buyer may recover all damages, however long it waited.
oe: Correct. Section 2-610: the aggrieved party may await performance for a commercially reasonable time or resort to remedies (§§ 2-703, 2-711), and in either case suspend its own performance. Substantial impairment is the same test as for installment contracts (cmt. 3).
Section 2-610(b) allows remedies even after urging retraction.
It may suspend its own performance.
Damages it should have avoided by acting within a commercially reasonable time aren't recoverable.
topic: Wk 8 · Termination, insecurity & repudiation — Options after repudiation

q: A seller repudiates in May a contract calling for delivery in August. In June, before the buyer has done anything in response, the seller writes, “We've reconsidered and will deliver in August as agreed.” The buyer had earlier sent a justified written demand for adequate assurance, which the seller's letter doesn't address. Is the retraction effective?
o: Not yet, because it lacks the demanded assurance.
Yes: a repudiating party may retract at any time before the performance date.
No: a repudiation can never be retracted.
Yes, because the buyer hasn't yet covered.
oe: Correct. Section 2-611(1)–(2). Once effective, retraction reinstates the repudiator's rights, with due allowance for delay (subsection (3)).
Retraction must include justifiably demanded assurances.
Section 2-611 allows retraction.
Lack of change of position is necessary but not sufficient.
topic: Wk 8 · Termination, insecurity & repudiation — Retraction

q: A buyer believes a seller has repudiated, cancels the contract, and buys from another supplier. A court later finds that the seller's statements were merely a request for a price increase, not a repudiation. What is the most likely consequence?
o: The buyer is in breach for cancelling wrongfully.
The seller is in breach, because its statements caused the confusion.
Neither is in breach, because the buyer acted in good faith.
The contract is rescinded by mutual mistake.
oe: Correct. It's sometimes hard to tell whether repudiation occurred, the “game of chicken.” A party that suspends or cancels on a mistaken belief risks being the breaching party; first pin down each side's obligations, and consider a § 2-609 demand.
A request for more isn't a repudiation; the buyer's cancellation was wrongful.
Good faith doesn't excuse a wrongful cancellation.
The buyer's misjudgment isn't a mutual mistake.
topic: Wk 8 · Termination, insecurity & repudiation — Game of chicken

q: A buyer with no reasonable grounds for insecurity sends the seller a written demand for “adequate assurance” and announces it is suspending payments. What is the likely result?
o: No right to suspend; possibly a repudiation.
The buyer may suspend payments for up to 30 days.
The seller must respond within 30 days or be in repudiation.
Nothing, because § 2-609 demands have no legal effect.
oe: Correct. The flowchart: no reasonable grounds → a request for assurance could be a repudiation; grounds but no written demand → no right to suspend; written demand for more than adequate assurance → can be a repudiation; proper demand → may suspend until adequate assurance arrives.
Only a justified demand allows suspension.
An unjustified demand doesn't trigger § 2-609(4).
A justified demand has effects, and an unjustified one carries risks for the demander.
topic: Wk 8 · Termination, insecurity & repudiation — The flowchart

q: A buyer contracted for specially tooled valves in six quarterly installments and advanced 25% of the price. Two weeks before the first delivery, the seller emails that the buyer's drawings were incomplete, it must retool, it can't deliver the first installment on time, “we expect you will cover the extra expenses,” and it expects to catch up by the second installment. The buyer now realizes it needs only half the valves and wants to cancel. What do you advise?
o: Don't cancel yet; demand adequate assurance in writing.
Cancel immediately and demand the 25% back, because any late installment is a repudiation of the whole contract.
Pay the extra costs to keep the contract alive.
Cancel, because the buyer overestimated its needs and may reduce the order.
oe: Correct. Problem 6-5: the late-first-installment statement repudiates that installment, but cancelling the whole requires substantial impairment of the whole contract (§§ 2-610, 2-612). The expense request is ambiguous. Over-ordering is the buyer's risk, and using the delay to escape it raises good-faith concerns. If the seller conditions performance on payment or fails to give adequate assurance within 30 days, the buyer may cancel, recover the 25%, and cover.
Substantial impairment of the whole is required.
The buyer needn't pay more than the contract requires.
Overestimating needs is the buyer's risk in a fixed-quantity contract.
topic: Wk 8 · Termination, insecurity & repudiation — Ace Supply valves

q: An art dealer contracts in writing to sell a specific Picasso etching to a buyer for $75,000; the buyer will return the next day with a cashier's check to pick it up. That night, lightning strikes the gallery and fire destroys the etching. Neither party was at fault. What are the parties' obligations?
o: The contract is avoided, and neither party owes anything.
The buyer must pay, because the contract was signed and the etching was identified.
The dealer must pay the buyer damages for failing to deliver.
The dealer must find and deliver a comparable Picasso etching.
oe: Correct. The merchant dealer still had the risk (no receipt, § 2-509(3)). Section 2-613 applies: goods identified when the contract was made, total casualty, no fault, before risk passed (Problem 6-6(a)).
Risk hadn't passed to the buyer, so the buyer owes nothing.
Section 2-613 avoids the contract, so no damages are owed.
Unique identified goods aren't replaceable; the contract is avoided.
topic: Wk 8 · Excuse from performance — Casualty to identified goods

q: Variation: The fire started from a coffee pot the dealer's employee carelessly left on overnight. What result?
o: No excuse: the dealer's negligence counts as fault.
The contract is still avoided, because the dealer didn't intend the fire.
The buyer bears the loss, because it delayed pickup until the next day.
The parties split the loss because the employee, not the dealer, was careless.
oe: Correct. Comment 1 to § 2-613. A wiring short would depend on whether the dealer negligently maintained it; lightning is no-fault.
Fault includes negligence, not just intentional wrongs.
The merchant dealer had the risk, and its negligence caused the loss.
An employee's negligence is the dealer's fault for this purpose.
topic: Wk 8 · Excuse from performance — Fault and § 2-613
pre: An art dealer contracts in writing to sell a specific Picasso etching to a buyer for $75,000; the buyer will return the next day with a cashier's check to pick it up. That night, lightning strikes the gallery and fire destroys the etching. Neither party was at fault. What are the parties' obligations?

q: Variation: The etching wasn't destroyed. It turns out it had been stolen years earlier, unknown to the dealer, and the rightful owner reclaims it before the buyer returns. Does § 2-613 excuse the dealer?
o: No: it's a title problem, and the dealer is in breach.
Yes: losing the goods to their true owner is a casualty without fault.
Yes, because the dealer bought the etching in good faith.
No, but the buyer bears the loss because it hadn't yet paid.
oe: Correct. Problem 6-6(b): § 2-613 doesn't excuse a seller that didn't own what it sold. The title warranty (§ 2-312) would have been breached had it delivered.
A third party's ownership claim isn't a casualty to the goods.
A thief's title is void, so good faith doesn't help.
The dealer bears it and is in breach.
topic: Wk 8 · Excuse from performance — Stolen etching
pre: An art dealer contracts in writing to sell a specific Picasso etching to a buyer for $75,000; the buyer will return the next day with a cashier's check to pick it up. That night, lightning strikes the gallery and fire destroys the etching. Neither party was at fault. What are the parties' obligations?

q: A dealer contracts to sell print #10 from a numbered series. Water damages print #10 without anyone's fault before risk passes. The dealer has an undamaged print #12 from the same series. What are the buyer's options if the contract required print #10 specifically?
o: Avoid the contract or accept #10 with a price allowance.
The buyer may demand print #12 at the contract price.
The buyer must accept print #10 at the full price.
The buyer may accept #10 and sue the dealer for damages.
oe: Correct. Section 2-613(b) governs partial loss of identified goods. If the prints were interchangeable (effectively fungible), the contract wouldn't require identified goods, there'd be no excuse, and the dealer would have to tender #12 (Problem 6-6(c)–(d)).
If #10 was specifically required, the dealer isn't obligated to substitute.
The buyer may choose avoidance or an allowance.
Accepting with an allowance means no further right against the seller.
topic: Wk 8 · Excuse from performance — Partial loss and substitutes

q: A contract calls for wheat to be shipped on a particular steamship line, which cancels all sailings without either party's fault. Shipment by another line from the same dock is available at slightly higher cost. The seller claims it's excused. What result?
o: Not excused: it must use the reasonable substitute.
The seller is excused, because the agreed carrier became unavailable.
The buyer may refuse the substitute and cancel.
The seller is excused unless the buyer pays the extra cost.
oe: Correct. Section 2-614(1) is a substitution rule, not an excuse (cmt. 1's Kosmos Steamer example; Hansen-Mueller v. Gau, where a buyer breached by refusing a substitute delivery point during flooding).
An available substitute must be used.
The buyer must accept a commercially reasonable substitute.
Higher cost alone doesn't excuse, and nothing shifts the cost to the buyer.
topic: Wk 8 · Excuse from performance — Substitute delivery

q: A plumber agreed to pay a supplier by funds transfer from a specific bank. Regulators seize the bank and freeze the plumber's account. The supplier is ready to deliver. The plumber claims it's excused. What result?
o: Not excused: it must offer an equivalent means of payment.
The plumber is excused, because the failure was caused by the government.
The supplier must deliver and wait until the account is unfrozen.
The contract is avoided under § 2-613.
oe: Correct. Section 2-614(2) (Problem 6-8(b)). If delivery had already been taken, payment by the means the regulation provides would discharge the buyer unless the regulation is discriminatory, oppressive, or predatory.
Section 2-614(2) doesn't excuse the buyer.
The supplier may withhold delivery absent a substitute payment.
Section 2-613 concerns casualty to identified goods.
topic: Wk 8 · Excuse from performance — Failed payment mechanism

q: A manufacturer contracts to supply rotor blades at a fixed price. A market boom triples the price of the metal it needs. The manufacturer claims excuse under § 2-615. What result?
o: No excuse: market increases are assumed risks.
Excused, because tripling costs makes performance commercially impracticable.
Excused, but only if the manufacturer notifies the buyer.
Excused if the buyer could have foreseen the price increase.
oe: Correct. Comment 4. Capacity events (war, embargo, local crop failure, unforeseen shutdown of major supply sources) can excuse; market events don't (Problem 6-7(A)(1)).
Market price changes are the classic assumed risk.
Notice doesn't create an excuse where none exists.
Foreseeability of a market change doesn't shift the risk to the buyer.
topic: Wk 8 · Excuse from performance — Market changes

q: Which event is most likely to excuse a rotor-blade manufacturer under § 2-615, assuming it gives notice?
o: An industry-wide metal workers' strike.
A sharp rise in the market price of metal.
A strike by the manufacturer's own employees over wages.
A rail strike, when shipping by truck is available at higher cost.
oe: Correct. A shutdown of major sources of supply is a capacity event within § 2-615 (cmt. 4). A strike by the manufacturer's own employees generally isn't an excuse; a rail strike calls for substitute trucking under § 2-614(1); a fire at its only plant may excuse if no fault and not an assumed risk (Problem 6-7(A)(2)–(5)).
Market changes don't excuse.
That's generally within the seller's control or assumed risk.
A reasonable substitute must be used under § 2-614(1).
topic: Wk 8 · Excuse from performance — Capacity events

q: A seller's contract contemplated a single named mine as its source of ore. A collapse shuts the mine. Which statement is most accurate?
o: Excuse only if it took due measures to secure the source.
The seller is automatically excused, because the contemplated source failed.
The contract is avoided under § 2-613, because the ore was identified.
The seller is never excused when a supplier fails.
oe: Correct. Comment 5: failure of an exclusive or contemplated source of supply through casualty falls under § 2-615, not § 2-613. Also, no excuse if the contingency was foreseen enough to be part of the dickered risks (cmt. 8), and a seller that causes governmental interference loses the exemption (cmt. 10).
Due measures are required.
Ore from a source isn't goods identified when the contract was made; § 2-615 governs.
Failure of a contemplated source can excuse if the seller took due measures.
topic: Wk 8 · Excuse from performance — Source of supply

q: A meteor storm damages a manufacturer's only plant without fault. It has 60,000 blades left but contracts for 60,000 with one customer and 120,000 with another. The first customer offers a premium for all 60,000. What must the manufacturer do?
o: Allocate fairly and notify each buyer of its quota.
Sell all 60,000 to the customer offering the premium.
Fill the earlier contract first in full.
Nothing, because partial capacity loss doesn't trigger any duty.
oe: Correct. Section 2-615(b)–(c). Giving everything to the highest bidder or to one favored customer is likely unfair; regular customers may be considered, and when prices have advanced, contract customers should be favored and supplies prorated (cmt. 11) (Problem 6-7(B)).
Allocation must be fair, not to the highest bidder.
First-in-time isn't required; fairness governs.
Section 2-615(b) addresses exactly that situation.
topic: Wk 8 · Excuse from performance — Allocation

q: A seller properly notifies a buyer under § 2-615 that it can supply only 40% of the next delivery. The buyer doesn't respond. Fifty days pass. What happens?
o: The contract lapses as to the affected deliveries.
The buyer is deemed to have accepted the 40% quota.
The seller must deliver 100% once it recovers.
The buyer may still terminate the entire contract at any time.
oe: Correct. Section 2-616(1)–(2): the buyer may, by written notice, terminate the unexecuted portion or modify by taking its quota; failing to modify within 30 days, the contract lapses as to the deliveries concerned. These rights can't be negated except to the extent the seller assumed a greater obligation (subsection (3)).
Silence leads to lapse, not acceptance.
The affected deliveries lapse.
Termination of the whole requires substantial impairment of the whole (§ 2-612).
topic: Wk 8 · Excuse from performance — Buyer's response to allocation

q: A plumber, low bidder on a town's new sewer system, contracts with a local supplier for 12,000 fittings that connect homes to a central sewer and have no other use. The town then cancels the project as too expensive. Is the plumber likely entitled to relief?
o: Likely yes, under frustration of purpose.
No: § 2-615 speaks only of sellers, so buyers can never be excused.
No: a fixed-price contract always allocates this risk to the buyer.
Yes, automatically, because governmental action excuses all parties.
oe: Correct. Problem 6-8(a): § 1-103(b) brings in Restatement § 265; § 2-615 cmt. 9 suggests its reasoning may exempt a buyer whose contract is conditioned on a definite venture. Counter: the plumber contracted before the town's final commitment, a risk it could have allocated.
Common-law frustration applies, and cmt. 9 extends § 2-615's reasoning.
Carbon County Coal involved market risk, not the collapse of a specific shared venture.
The town's decision supports frustration, but relief isn't automatic.
topic: Wk 8 · Excuse from performance — Frustration of purpose

q: A utility signs a long-term fixed-price contract to buy coal. Electricity demand falls and cheaper power becomes available, so the coal is now worth far less to the utility. It seeks excuse. Under Northern Indiana Public Service v. Carbon County Coal, what result?
o: No excuse: the buyer bore the market risk.
Excuse under § 2-615, because the market collapse was unforeseeable.
Excuse under frustration, because the contract became unprofitable.
Excuse under § 2-613, because the coal lost its value.
oe: Correct. Judge Posner: excuse doctrines have no place when the contract assigns the risk. Contrast International Minerals v. Llano, where a new environmental regulation prevented the buyer's use (Restatement § 264).
Market changes are allocated by fixed-price contracts.
Unprofitability isn't frustration.
Section 2-613 concerns physical casualty to identified goods.
topic: Wk 8 · Excuse from performance — Buyer's market risk

q: Which statement best reflects the course's view of excuse doctrines?
o: Excuse is applied sparingly, as a risk allocation.
Any unforeseeable event that makes performance more expensive excuses a seller.
Excuse doctrines decide who bears the loss of destroyed goods.
A foreseeable risk can never be the basis for excuse.
oe: Correct. Speciality Tires v. CIT: “foreseeability or even recognition of a risk does not necessarily prove its allocation” (ALCOA). If a flood sweeps away the car before risk passes, an excused seller loses the car but owes no damages; an unexcused one loses the car and owes damages.
Increased cost alone doesn't excuse.
That's risk of loss; excuse decides who pays damages.
Foreseeability is important but not dispositive.

q: A sole-proprietor artisan who contracted to hand-make custom furniture dies before finishing it. Separately, a new statute makes it illegal to sell a product a seller had contracted to deliver. Which law supplies the excuse rules?
o: The Restatement, through § 1-103(b).
Section 2-613, because both events make the goods unavailable.
Section 2-614, because both obstruct delivery.
Neither event can excuse performance under any law.
oe: Correct. The chart maps casualty to identified goods to § 2-613 (R2d § 263), obstruction of delivery to § 2-614(1), obstruction of payment to § 2-614(2), and production problems to §§ 2-615/2-616 (R2d § 261). Death and intervening illegality have no Article 2 rule.
Section 2-613 covers casualty to identified goods.
Section 2-614 covers delivery facilities and payment means.
Restatement §§ 262 and 264 address exactly these.

q: A seller's contract says: “Seller assumes all risks of supply disruption and will perform regardless of any contingency.” A war cuts off its only supply source. Can it claim § 2-615 excuse?
o: Likely not: it assumed a greater obligation.
Yes: § 2-615 can't be waived by agreement.
Yes, because war is always an excusing event.
No, but the buyer must still give the seller 30 days to perform.
oe: Correct. Sections 2-613 to 2-615 are subject to contrary agreement. By contrast, the buyer's § 2-616 procedure can't be negated except to the extent the seller assumed a greater obligation.
It expressly yields to a seller's assumption of a greater obligation.
Not if the seller assumed the risk.
The 30-day rule is the buyer's response window under § 2-616.
